practice_questions.text: State Hooke's law in terms of force and extension.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied (provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded). Accept F = ke with terms defined.

practice_questions.text: A spring has a natural length of 10 cm. When a 4 N force is applied, the spring has a length of 14 cm. Calculate the spring constant.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for finding extension: e = 14 − 10 = 4 cm = 0.04 m. 1 mark for correct answer: k = F/e = 4/0.04 = 100 N/m (with unit).

practice_questions.text: A student plots a force-extension graph for a spring. Describe the shape of the graph (i) below the limit of proportionality and (ii) beyond the limit of proportionality. For each, explain what this tells us about the spring.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: (i) Straight line through the origin — extension is directly proportional to force, spring obeys Hooke's law (2 marks). (ii) Graph curves / gradient increases — extension increases more rapidly per newton of force, Hooke's law no longer applies, spring may be permanently deformed (2 marks). Secure: Both sections described and linked to behaviour. Developing: Straight line described correctly but curvature section vague. Emerging: Mentions graph changes shape only.

practice_questions.text: A spring with a spring constant of 150 N/m is compressed by 0.04 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct substitution: Epe = 0.5 × 150 × (0.04)². 1 mark for correct answer: Epe = 0.5 × 150 × 0.0016 = 0.12 J (with unit).

practice_questions.text: Describe the core practical procedure used to investigate how the extension of a spring varies with force. Include the measurements taken, how the spring constant is found from the results, and one source of error and how to reduce it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Hang spring from clamp stand; measure natural length (1 mark); add masses of known weight (F = mg) one at a time and record total length after each addition (1 mark); calculate extension = new length − natural length (1 mark); plot force-extension graph and find k from gradient of straight-line section (1 mark); parallax error when reading ruler — use set square or pointer at eye level to reduce it (1 mark); repeat measurements and average to improve reliability (1 mark). Secure: 4–5 points present. Developing: Procedure described but method for finding k missing or error not clearly addressed. Emerging: Some steps mentioned without structure.

practice_questions.text: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is stretched by 0.15 m and then released, launching a ball of mass 0.040 kg vertically. Calculate (a) the elastic potential energy stored in the spring and (b) the maximum speed of the ball, assuming all elastic potential energy converts to kinetic energy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: (a) Epe = 0.5 × 200 × (0.15)² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.0225 = 2.25 J (2 marks for correct method + answer with unit). (b) Set Epe = Ek: 2.25 = 0.5 × 0.040 × v²; v² = 2.25/0.02 = 112.5; v = 10.6 m/s (3 s.f.) (2 marks for correct method + answer with unit). State assumption: all elastic PE converts to KE (1 mark). Secure: (a) correct, (b) correct method but arithmetic error or unit omitted. Developing: (a) correct, (b) sets up equation but cannot rearrange. Emerging: Correct formula stated for (a) but wrong substitution.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates how concentration affects the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid. She uses five different concentrations and measures the time for a cross to disappear each time. Describe the method she should use, including how she will make her results reliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear chronological method including: labelling independent variable (concentration of thiosulfate), dependent variable (time for cross to disappear), at least two controls (volume of solutions, same cross, same viewing height, temperature); states repeats and calculation of mean; explains how rate = 1/time.
Secure: Method described with IV and DV; at least one control stated; mentions repeats; may lack rate calculation or one control variable.
Developing: Basic method described; IV or DV not clearly named; some controls missing; repeats may be absent.
Emerging: General description of mixing chemicals; little or no reference to variables or reliable results.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using collision theory, why increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States particles gain more kinetic energy; move faster; collide more frequently; AND a greater proportion of collisions have energy greater than or equal to activation energy; all four points clearly linked.
Secure: Three of the four collision theory points clearly linked.
Developing: States particles collide more often but does not distinguish between frequency and energy of collisions.
Emerging: States temperature makes particles move faster with no collision theory link.

practice_questions.text: In an experiment, marble chips of mass 5 g react with 50 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. A student repeats the experiment using the same mass of marble chips ground to a fine powder. Explain the difference in rate of reaction between the two experiments.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies greater surface area in powdered chips; more area exposed to acid particles; collision frequency increases; rate increases — all four points linked.
Secure: Greater surface area leads to more collisions; rate increases; may not explicitly link to exposure of more solid particles to acid.
Developing: States powder reacts faster and gives surface area as reason, but without collision theory link.
Emerging: States powder reacts faster with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the initial rate of reaction if 48 cm³ of gas is collected in the first 60 seconds. Give your answer with units.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct substitution (48 ÷ 60). 1 mark: answer 0.8 cm³/s with correct units. Allow equivalent units (e.g. cm³ s⁻¹).

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term activation energy.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the minimum energy that (colliding) particles must have for a reaction to occur (for a collision to be successful).

practice_questions.text: Compare the two methods used in the core practical for investigating reaction rates. Include: what is measured, an advantage of each method, and how each gives a value for rate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly contrasts gas syringe (measures volume of CO₂) vs cross timing (measures time for precipitate to appear); gives a genuine advantage of each (gas syringe gives continuous data; cross timing is simple and cheap); explains how rate is extracted (gradient or 1/time); language is precise throughout.
Secure: Both methods described with what is measured; one advantage stated; rate extraction partially explained for both.
Developing: One method described in detail; second mentioned but not compared.
Emerging: One method described only with no comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is correct about photosynthesis?
A) It is an exothermic reaction that releases energy
B) It takes place in the mitochondria of plant cells
C) It is an endothermic reaction that absorbs light energy
D) It produces carbon dioxide and water as products
practice_questions.marks: C) It is an endothermic reaction that absorbs light energy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) A student places pondweed at a distance of 10 cm from a lamp and counts 40 bubbles per minute. They then move the lamp to 20 cm.

Using the inverse square law, calculate the predicted rate of photosynthesis at 20 cm. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
• Distance doubles, so intensity = 1 ÷ 2² = 1/4 of original [1 mark]
• New rate = 40 × 1/4 = 10 bubbles per minute [1 mark]
• Units stated correctly (bubbles per minute) [1 mark]
[3 marks] — ECF: if incorrect ratio used but calculation is consistent, award ECF on final answer

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates the effect of CO₂ concentration on the rate of photosynthesis at two light intensities (high and low).

Explain what would happen to the rate of photosynthesis at high light intensity as CO₂ concentration is increased from very low to very high.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At low CO₂, rate is low because CO₂ is the limiting factor; increasing CO₂ increases the rate as more raw material is available; rate continues to rise; eventually light or temperature becomes the new limiting factor; rate plateaus at a level determined by the next limiting factor — student links each change causally.
Secure: Rate increases as CO₂ increases; plateau explained as another factor becoming limiting.
Developing: Rate increases mentioned; plateau stated but reason not explained.
Emerging: Simple statement that more CO₂ means more photosynthesis.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the method a student should use to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using pondweed. Include the variables and how to ensure the results are reliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Independent variable — lamp distance from plant; dependent variable — bubble count per minute (or O₂ sensor reading); controls — temperature (water bath), CO₂ concentration (sodium hydrogen carbonate solution), same plant cutting; equilibrate at each distance before recording; repeat each distance 3+ times and calculate mean; plot rate vs distance or vs 1/d²; thermometer measures temperature — water bath controls it.
Secure: At least four of: IV, DV, two controls, repeats, equilibration, analysis method.
Developing: Basic method described; at least two variables identified; some mention of repeats.
Emerging: Partial method; few control variables; no analysis plan.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text: Explain why plants use glucose produced during photosynthesis for more than just respiration.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any three of:
• Converting glucose to starch for storage in roots and leaves.
• Synthesising cellulose for cell wall construction.
• Combining glucose derivatives with mineral ions (nitrates) to make amino acids and proteins.
• Converting glucose to lipids for storage in seeds or for membranes.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A gardener wants to maximise the growth rate of tomato plants in a greenhouse. Suggest and explain two changes the gardener could make to increase the rate of photosynthesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For each suggestion — one mark for the change, one mark for the mechanism. E.g.: Increase artificial lighting (increase light intensity) → more light energy available to drive photosynthesis beyond the current limiting level. Add CO₂ burners → increased CO₂ concentration means more raw material available for the Calvin cycle. Raise temperature to ~25–30°C → enzyme-controlled reactions proceed faster up to the optimum temperature. Student explains mechanism for each.
Secure: Two valid suggestions with partial mechanism.
Developing: One fully explained suggestion; one partially explained.
Emerging: Suggestions only, no mechanism.
[4 marks — 2 marks per suggestion: 1 for change, 1 for mechanism]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'isotope'.
practice_questions.marks: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons (same atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass numbers). Accept: same element, different mass number.

practice_questions.text: An atom of fluorine has atomic number 9 and mass number 19. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in this atom.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: 9 protons. 1 mark: 10 neutrons (19 − 9). 1 mark: 9 electrons (equals number of protons in a neutral atom).

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Boron has two naturally occurring isotopes: boron-10 (20% abundance) and boron-11 (80% abundance). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Correct calculation: (20 × 10 + 80 × 11) ÷ 100 = (200 + 880) ÷ 100 = 1080 ÷ 100. 1 mark: Final answer 10.8 (no unit required for relative atomic mass).

practice_questions.text: Describe Rutherford's gold foil experiment and explain how the results disproved the plum pudding model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes alpha particles fired at thin gold foil; detector records deflections; most pass straight through (atom is mostly empty space); a small number are deflected at large angles (positively charged nucleus repels positive alpha particles); very few bounce back (nucleus is very dense and small); plum pudding model predicted only slight deflections; the result disproved it because a diffuse positive charge could not cause large deflections; new nuclear model proposed with dense central nucleus.
Secure: Describes the experiment and links at least two observations to conclusions about atomic structure.
Developing: Describes the experiment and states that the result led to the nuclear model, with one observational link.
Emerging: Describes the experiment broadly without connecting results to model change.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Dalton's claim that 'all atoms of an element are identical' is an oversimplification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Isotopes of the same element exist — they have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. 1 mark: Isotopes therefore have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, meaning atoms of the same element are not identical in mass.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how the discovery of the electron and the neutron each contributed to improving scientific models of the atom. Refer to named scientists in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses Thomson's discovery of the electron (1897) and resulting plum pudding model — strength: first evidence of internal structure; limitation: failed to account for the concentrated nucleus; Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1909–1911) replaced it with the nuclear model; Chadwick's discovery of the neutron (1932) — explained mass discrepancy and the existence of isotopes; evaluates how each discovery was driven by new experimental evidence; discusses how each model improved on the last; considers whether science ever produces a 'complete' model; justified conclusion.
Secure: Named scientists, their discoveries, and how each refined the model, with evaluative reasoning and a conclusion.
Developing: Names at least three scientists and their contributions with limited evaluation.
Emerging: Lists scientists without explaining how their discoveries changed models.

practice_questions.text:
Which equation correctly represents power?
A) P = Fd
B) P = mv²
C) P = E/t
D) P = mgh
practice_questions.marks: C) P = E/t [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation for work done and give the unit of work done.
practice_questions.marks: W = F × d (or W = Fd), and the unit is the joule (J). [1 mark for both parts correct]

practice_questions.text: A shopping trolley is pushed with a force of 35 N across a car park. The trolley moves 20 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.
practice_questions.marks:
W = F × d [1 mark for correct substitution]
W = 35 × 20 = 700 J [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: A skier of mass 65 kg descends from a height of 120 m to the bottom of a slope. Assuming no energy is lost to friction or air resistance, calculate the speed of the skier at the bottom of the slope. (g = 10 N/kg)
practice_questions.marks:
GPE at top = KE at bottom:
mgh = ½mv² [1 mark for stating or using this relationship]
65 × 10 × 120 = ½ × 65 × v² [1 mark for correct substitution]
78 000 = 32.5v²
v² = 2400
v = 49 m/s (to 2 s.f.) [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: An electric winch raises a crate of mass 200 kg through a height of 8 m in 20 seconds. Calculate (i) the work done on the crate and (ii) the power of the winch. (g = 10 N/kg)
practice_questions.marks:
Part (i):
W = mgh = 200 × 10 × 8 [1 mark for correct method]
W = 16 000 J (16 kJ) [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

Part (ii):
P = W/t [1 mark for correct equation]
P = 16 000 ÷ 20 [1 mark for correct substitution]
P = 800 W [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

[1 mark for consistent use of units throughout, or correct ECF from part (i) into part (ii)]

practice_questions.text: A car travelling at constant speed of 30 m/s experiences total resistive forces of 2400 N. Explain why the engine must do work continuously, and calculate the power output of the engine at this speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation that at constant speed the driving force equals resistive force (Newton's first law); P = Fv correctly applied with answer 72 000 W (72 kW) and correct unit; explanation links work done to energy dissipated as thermal energy by friction/air resistance.
Secure: Correct P = Fv calculation (72 kW); explanation covers constant speed requires equal forces; minor omission in energy explanation.
Developing: Partially correct calculation with some method shown; states that force is needed to overcome friction without full Newton's first law framing.
Emerging: Restates that the car is moving or that the engine works; no valid calculation.

Answer: Driving force = 2400 N (equals resistive force at constant speed). P = Fv = 2400 × 30 = 72 000 W = 72 kW. This work is done against resistive forces and transferred to the thermal energy stores of the air, brakes, and tyres.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is found in a prokaryotic cell but NOT in a eukaryotic cell?
A) Mitochondria
B) Ribosome
C) Plasmid
D) Cell membrane
practice_questions.marks: C) Plasmid [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the function of the permanent vacuole in a plant cell.
practice_questions.marks: Contains cell sap / keeps the cell turgid / supports the cell structure. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student views an onion cell under a light microscope. The image of the cell measures 24 mm. The actual size of the cell is 0.04 mm.
Calculate the magnification used. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Magnification = image size ÷ real size [1 mark]
Magnification = 24 ÷ 0.04 = ×600 [1 mark]
(Accept correct working with answer in any equivalent form; mark cannot be awarded without a numerical answer.)

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the structure of a sperm cell is adapted to its function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear adaptations each with a full causal explanation, e.g. 'The midpiece is packed with mitochondria, which carry out aerobic respiration to transfer energy for the movement of the flagellum' and 'The acrosome contains enzymes that digest the egg cell membrane, allowing the sperm nucleus to enter and fertilise the egg.' (4 marks)
Secure: Two adaptations with partial explanation, e.g. 'Many mitochondria to provide energy for swimming; long flagellum for movement.' (3 marks)
Developing: One well-explained adaptation or two stated without explanation. (2 marks)
Emerging: One simple statement with limited science. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use a light microscope to prepare and view a sample of cheek cells. Include how to obtain a clear, well-focused image.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Chronological method covering: smear cells on slide, add methylene blue stain to make nuclei visible, lower coverslip at an angle (to prevent air bubbles distorting image), clip slide on stage, begin on lowest power objective, use coarse focus then fine focus to sharpen image, switch to higher power using fine focus only. Control variable stated (e.g. same stain concentration). (6 marks)
Secure: Covers most key steps including stain use, coverslip technique and focusing sequence. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Several steps present but gaps in method (e.g. no mention of stain or air bubble prevention). (2–3 marks)
Emerging: Basic procedure described without key details. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: A bacterium has a diameter of 3 μm. Express this measurement in metres, giving your answer in standard form.
practice_questions.marks:
Conversion: 3 μm = 3 × 10⁻⁶ m [1 mark for correct conversion, 1 mark for correct standard form]
(Accept 3 × 10⁻⁶ m. Do not accept 0.000003 m alone without standard form.)

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a vector quantity?
A) Temperature
B) Mass
C) Speed
D) Force
practice_questions.marks: D) Force [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the principle of moments.
practice_questions.marks: For an object in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any pivot equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same pivot. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A spanner of length 0.25 m is used to turn a bolt. A force of 80 N is applied perpendicular to the spanner. Calculate the moment produced.
practice_questions.marks:
M = F × d [1 mark for correct equation or substitution]
M = 80 × 0.25 = 20 N m [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: A uniform beam of length 4 m is balanced on a pivot at its centre. A weight of 60 N is placed 1.5 m to the left of the pivot. Calculate the weight that must be placed 1.0 m to the right of the pivot to balance the beam.
practice_questions.marks:
Anticlockwise moment = 60 × 1.5 = 90 N m [1 mark]
For balance: clockwise moment = 90 N m [1 mark for applying principle of moments]
W × 1.0 = 90
W = 90 N [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: A student uses a metre rule balanced on a pivot at its 50 cm mark to investigate the principle of moments. Describe how the student could use this equipment to find the weight of a stone, using a 1 N standard weight.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear method including: balance rule horizontally on pivot; hang standard 1 N weight on one side at a known distance; hang stone on opposite side; adjust distances until balanced; apply principle of moments to calculate stone's weight (W × d₁ = 1 × d₂ → W = d₂/d₁ N); state variables controlled (same pivot position, rule horizontal) and how to repeat for reliability.
Secure: Correct method with moments equation applied; may miss one control variable or repeat.
Developing: Describes hanging weights and adjusting distances; does not apply moments equation clearly.
Emerging: Describes a balance or weighing without applying moments reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
A driving gear with 15 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 45 teeth. The driving gear rotates at 600 rpm.
(i) Calculate the speed of the driven gear.
(ii) Explain the effect on the turning force (torque) applied by the driven gear compared with the driving gear.
practice_questions.marks:
(i) Speed of driven = (15/45) × 600 = 200 rpm [1 mark for correct ratio; 1 mark for correct answer with unit]
(ii) The driven gear has more teeth and rotates more slowly [1 mark]; as a result it applies a greater torque (turning force) than the driving gear — three times greater in this case [1 mark]. Speed and force trade off: what is lost in speed is gained in torque.

practice_questions.text: State the equation for pressure in a fluid at depth h.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: p = hρg (or pressure = depth × density × gravitational field strength). Accept p = hρg with symbols defined.

practice_questions.text: A submarine descends to a depth of 150 m in the sea. The density of sea water is 1020 kg/m³. Taking g = 9.8 N/kg, calculate the pressure due to the water column at this depth.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct substitution: p = 150 × 1020 × 9.8. 1 mark for correct answer: p = 1,499,400 Pa (accept 1.5 × 10⁶ Pa or 1500 kPa, with unit).

practice_questions.text: A block of wood with a volume of 0.002 m³ is fully submerged in fresh water (density 1000 kg/m³). The weight of the block is 12 N. Taking g = 9.8 N/kg, calculate the upthrust and determine whether the block will float or sink when released.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct upthrust calculation: upthrust = 1000 × 0.002 × 9.8 = 19.6 N. 1 mark for comparison: upthrust (19.6 N) > weight (12 N). 1 mark for correct conclusion: the block will float (rise to the surface).

practice_questions.text: Explain why atmospheric pressure decreases as you travel higher above sea level.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of air above (1 mark); at higher altitude, less air sits above (1 mark); therefore less weight pressing down (1 mark); so pressure is lower (1 mark). Secure: Three points correctly linked. Developing: States pressure decreases with altitude but explanation limited to 'there is less air'. Emerging: Vague reference to altitude affecting pressure without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: A large steel ship floats in sea water, even though steel has a much greater density than sea water. Explain, in terms of upthrust, displaced fluid, and density, why the ship floats.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The ship's hull displaces a large volume of sea water (1 mark); upthrust equals the weight of sea water displaced (Archimedes' principle) (1 mark); the total volume of the ship (including air-filled interior) is large enough that the average density of the ship is less than sea water (1 mark); the weight of sea water displaced equals the total weight of the ship (1 mark); upthrust therefore equals weight and the ship is in equilibrium, floating (1 mark); if the ship is overloaded, the average density increases and upthrust may no longer balance weight, causing sinking (1 mark). Secure: 4–5 points with Archimedes' principle explicitly stated. Developing: Explains upthrust but does not relate to average density of ship. Emerging: States ship floats because of upthrust without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the total pressure experienced by a diver at a depth of 30 m in a freshwater lake. The density of fresh water is 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg, and atmospheric pressure is 101,000 Pa. Show your working clearly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for fluid pressure: p_fluid = 30 × 1000 × 9.8 = 294,000 Pa. 1 mark for adding atmospheric pressure: p_total = 294,000 + 101,000. 1 mark for correct answer: 395,000 Pa (accept 3.95 × 10⁵ Pa, with unit).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly states Newton's first law?
A) A force is needed to keep an object moving at constant velocity
B) Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
C) An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
D) Acceleration is proportional to mass
A 600 kg motorbike has a driving force of 3600 N and total resistive forces of 600 N. Calculate the acceleration of the motorbike.
Describe what happens to the speed and the forces acting on a skydiver from the moment they jump until they reach terminal velocity. Do not include the parachute opening.
practice_questions.marks: Speed increases (accelerates) initially [1]; as speed increases, drag increases [1]; when drag equals weight, resultant force is zero and terminal velocity is reached (constant speed) [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why braking distance increases much more than thinking distance when a driver doubles their speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear quantitative reasoning linking kinetic energy or stopping distance to speed squared.
Secure: Both distances addressed with causal explanation.
Developing: One distance explained; limited comparison.
Emerging: Simple relevant point.

Credit points:
• Thinking distance is directly proportional to speed [1]
• Doubling speed doubles thinking distance [1]
• Kinetic energy is proportional to speed² (Ek = ½mv²) [1]
• Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy, so braking distance more than doubles [1]

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) A 800 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s east collides with a stationary 400 kg crate. After the collision, the crate moves east at 8 m/s.
(a) Calculate the total momentum before the collision. [2]
(b) Calculate the velocity of the trolley after the collision. State the direction of motion. [2]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) p = mv = 800 × 6 = 4800 kg m/s (east) [1]; crate p = 0; total = 4800 kg m/s [1]
(b) Momentum after: crate = 400 × 8 = 3200 kg m/s; trolley momentum after = 4800 − 3200 = 1600 kg m/s [1]; v = 1600 / 800 = 2 m/s east [1].

practice_questions.text: A student investigates Newton's second law using a trolley, pulley, and hanging masses on a runway. Describe how the student should set up and carry out the investigation, including what measurements to take, how to ensure a fair test, and how to use the results to confirm Newton's second law.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Systematic method with IV, DV, controls, repeats, and analysis plan clearly linked to F = ma.
Secure: IV, DV, and controls identified; method mostly complete.
Developing: Some steps described but missing key controls or analysis.
Emerging: Simple relevant points.

Credit points (any 6):
• Attach string from trolley over pulley to hanging masses [1]
• Use light gates (or ticker timer) to measure time and calculate acceleration [1]
• Independent variable: force (number of masses on hanger) [1]
• Dependent variable: acceleration [1]
• Control: keep total mass of system constant (move masses from trolley to hanger, not add) [1]
• Carry out repeats and calculate mean acceleration for each force [1]
• Plot graph of F (y-axis) against a (x-axis) [1]
• Straight line through origin confirms F ∝ a, confirming Newton's second law [1]

practice_questions.text: What is meant by denaturation of an enzyme?
practice_questions.marks: A permanent change in the shape of the enzyme's active site [1 mark] so that the substrate can no longer bind / the enzyme can no longer function. (Do not accept 'the enzyme is destroyed' without reference to shape change.)

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates the effect of sucrose concentration on the mass of potato cylinders. The table shows her results:

Sucrose concentration (mol/dm³) | Initial mass (g) | Final mass (g)
0.0 | 2.8 | 3.2
0.2 | 2.9 | 3.0
0.6 | 3.1 | 2.8

Calculate the percentage change in mass for the 0.6 mol/dm³ solution. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage change = (2.8 − 3.1) ÷ 3.1 × 100 [1 mark for correct substitution]
= −9.7% (accept −9.68% to −9.7%) [1 mark for correct answer with negative sign indicating mass loss]

practice_questions.text:
A food sample is tested with Benedict's solution and heated in a water bath. The solution turns brick-red.
Identify which food molecule is present and explain what this colour change indicates.
practice_questions.marks:
Food molecule: reducing sugar (e.g. glucose) [1 mark]
Explanation: Benedict's reagent is reduced by the sugar, forming a brick-red copper(I) oxide precipitate [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why active transport requires energy but diffusion does not.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Diffusion moves particles down the concentration gradient (from high to low), which is energetically favourable and occurs spontaneously. Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient (from low to high), which is not spontaneous and requires energy from cellular respiration (ATP from mitochondria) to power carrier proteins. (4 marks)
Secure: Correct direction for both processes and energy source named (respiration/ATP). (3 marks)
Developing: Correct directions stated but energy source vague ('uses energy from cells'). (2 marks)
Emerging: One correct point, e.g. 'active transport moves against the gradient'. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the effect of temperature on amylase activity. Describe how she should carry out a fair investigation, including how to measure the rate of reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sets up water baths at a range of temperatures; adds buffer solution to starch-amylase mixture to control pH; uses iodine to test for starch at regular intervals; times how long until iodine no longer turns blue-black; calculates rate as 1/time; identifies independent variable (temperature), dependent variable (time for colour change), and controls (pH, starch and enzyme concentration, volume of solutions); repeats for reliability. (6 marks)
Secure: Correct method with most steps, states control variables and rate calculation. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Describes use of water bath and iodine test, but misses controls or rate calculation. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: Refers to temperature and iodine but little method detail. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
'Understanding enzyme denaturation is more useful to biology than understanding diffusion.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighs evidence on both sides. For denaturation: explains importance for understanding digestion, body temperature regulation, medical applications (e.g. fever, enzyme inhibitors as drugs). For diffusion: explains role in gas exchange, nutrient absorption, all passive transport in cells. Draws a justified conclusion with criteria stated (e.g. 'diffusion is more fundamental because every cell relies on it constantly, whereas denaturation is a pathological change'). Uses correct terminology throughout. (6 marks)
Secure: Both sides argued with specific biological examples; conclusion present but criteria less explicit. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Both processes described rather than evaluated; little comparison or conclusion. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: One process described with minimal evaluation. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: State two structural features of a root hair cell that make it well adapted for absorbing water from the soil.
practice_questions.marks:
For each correct point any two of:
• Long thin extension (root hair) greatly increases surface area for absorption.
• Thin cell wall and large surface area allow rapid osmosis.
• Many mitochondria to provide ATP for active transport of mineral ions (credit if linked to mineral absorption rather than water).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student measures water uptake by a leafy plant cutting using a potometer. The air bubble moves 6.0 cm in 4 minutes.

(a) Calculate the rate of water uptake in cm per minute.
(b) The student places the plant in a humid environment. Explain what they would expect to happen to the rate of water uptake and why.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Rate = 6.0 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cm per minute [1 mark — with units]
(b) Rate would decrease [1 mark]; because in humid air the concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the surrounding air is smaller, so water vapour diffuses out of stomata more slowly [1 mark].
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the structural differences between xylem and phloem, and explain why each structure is suited to its function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Xylem — dead cells, hollow lumen, lignified walls; function is to transport water and minerals upward under tension — dead hollow tubes prevent blockage and lignin provides strength; one direction only. Phloem — living cells with sieve plates; function is to transport dissolved sugars (translocation) from source to sink in both directions — living cells maintain active loading/unloading of sugars; sieve plates allow flow between cells.
Secure: At least one structural feature per tissue linked to its specific function.
Developing: Structural differences described without clear link to function.
Emerging: Correct substances named but structural detail absent.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how transpiration creates the transpiration stream, which moves water from the roots to the leaves.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Water evaporates from leaf cells through open stomata (transpiration); this lowers water potential in leaf mesophyll cells; water moves from xylem into these cells by osmosis; this creates tension (a pull) in the xylem column; cohesion between water molecules maintains an unbroken column; water is pulled up from the roots, drawing more water in by osmosis through root hair cells — full chain of cause and effect.
Secure: Water evaporation from leaves creates tension in xylem pulling water upward; water enters at roots by osmosis.
Developing: Transpiration described; water movement through xylem mentioned; mechanism incomplete.
Emerging: Water moves from roots to leaves; no mechanistic explanation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two adaptations of leaves that reduce unnecessary water loss, and explain how each adaptation works.
practice_questions.marks:
For each adaptation (2 marks each):
• Waxy cuticle on upper epidermis — waterproof layer reduces evaporation of water directly through the leaf surface.
• Stomata mainly on underside (lower epidermis) — away from direct sunlight and therefore cooler, reducing evaporation rate; also, when photosynthesis slows (e.g. at night), guard cells lose water and stomata close, preventing water loss.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A scientist investigates how wind speed affects the rate of transpiration by placing identical plant cuttings in a wind tunnel at different fan speeds and measuring water uptake with a potometer.

Explain why increasing wind speed increases the rate of transpiration, and suggest one variable that must be controlled to make the investigation valid.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf surface, maintaining a steep concentration gradient between the humid air inside the leaf (saturated near the stomata) and the drier air outside; steeper gradient means faster diffusion of water vapour out of stomata; this increases the rate of evaporation from leaf cells and pulls more water up the xylem. Control variable: temperature (or light intensity, or CO₂ concentration, or leaf surface area) — explained why it must be controlled (to ensure wind speed is the only variable affecting rate).
Secure: Concentration gradient explanation present; wind removes vapour; one valid control variable with justification.
Developing: Wind removes vapour; concentration gradient mentioned without full explanation; control variable named without justification.
Emerging: Wind speeds up water loss; no mechanism.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text: State why Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table.
practice_questions.marks: He predicted that elements had yet to be discovered that would fill the gaps (and whose properties would match predictions based on their position in the table).

practice_questions.text: Write the electronic configuration of phosphorus (atomic number 15) and identify which group and period it is in.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Electronic configuration 2, 8, 5. 1 mark: Group 5 (5 outer electrons). 1 mark: Period 3 (3 electron shells occupied).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the reactivity of Group 1 metals increases going down the group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Group 1 metals all have one electron in their outer shell; going down the group the outer shell is in an energy level further from the nucleus; the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron decreases; the electron is more easily lost; so the metal reacts more readily (is more reactive).
Secure: Three of the four points above with correct causal language.
Developing: States reactivity increases and mentions the outer electron being further from the nucleus without explaining attraction.
Emerging: States reactivity increases going down Group 1 only.

practice_questions.text: Chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium iodide. Describe and explain what you would observe, writing a symbol equation for the reaction.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The solution turns brown/dark orange. 1 mark: Iodine is produced — chlorine is more reactive than iodine and displaces it from the potassium iodide solution. 1 mark: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂ (allow word equation for this mark). 1 mark: Chlorine gains electrons more easily than iodine (its outer shell is closer to the nucleus, so it has a stronger pull on incoming electrons).

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of Group 1 metals with those of transition metals.
practice_questions.marks: Any four correct comparative points, one mark each: Group 1 are highly reactive / transition metals are much less reactive; Group 1 have low melting points / transition metals have high melting points; Group 1 are soft and low density / transition metals are hard and high density; Group 1 form colourless ionic compounds / transition metals form coloured compounds; transition metals (not Group 1) commonly act as catalysts.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the significance of Mendeleev's periodic table in the development of chemistry as a science. Refer to specific features of his table and how later discoveries confirmed or challenged his ideas.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains the historical context (elements classified by atomic weight before Mendeleev); evaluates Mendeleev's specific innovations (ordering by atomic weight, grouping by properties, gaps for undiscovered elements, swapping element positions); discusses the predictive success (gallium, germanium predicted before discovery and later confirmed); discusses how later work (discovery of atomic number and subatomic particles) refined rather than overturned his table; considers limitations (no explanation of why similar elements have similar properties — required electron theory); justified conclusion about the table's scientific importance.
Secure: Covers at least three features of Mendeleev's table, how predictions were confirmed and how the modern table differs, with a conclusion.
Developing: Describes Mendeleev's table and gaps for undiscovered elements with limited evaluation.
Emerging: Describes Mendeleev's contribution with few specific details.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) The Haber process uses a temperature of 450°C and a pressure of 200 atmospheres. Explain why these conditions represent a compromise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that low temperature favours forward exothermic reaction (better yield) but rate is too slow; 450°C balances acceptable yield with commercially viable rate; high pressure favours side with fewer moles of gas (right), improving yield; very high pressure is expensive and dangerous; 200 atm is a practical compromise. Catalyst noted as speeding up equilibrium without changing yield. All reasoning linked to Le Chatelier's principle.
Secure: Temperature compromise explained (rate vs yield); pressure compromise explained (fewer moles); catalyst role stated. At least four of six marks' worth of points present.
Developing: One condition explained with partial Le Chatelier link; second condition described but not explained.
Emerging: States conditions with no explanation of why they represent a compromise.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by dynamic equilibrium. In your answer, state two features of a system at dynamic equilibrium.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States system must be closed; rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal; concentrations of reactants and products are constant; reaction is still occurring in both directions (dynamic not static); all four features clearly explained.
Secure: Three of the four features clearly stated and explained.
Developing: Two features stated; may confuse constant concentrations with equal concentrations.
Emerging: States equilibrium is reached but gives no features or incorrect features.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) The equilibrium for ammonia synthesis is: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). Using Le Chatelier's principle, predict and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium of: (a) increasing the pressure, (b) increasing the temperature.
practice_questions.marks: (a) 1 mark: equilibrium shifts right (towards products / fewer moles of gas). 1 mark: because there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the system opposes the pressure increase by reducing moles. (b) 1 mark: equilibrium shifts left (towards reactants). 1 mark: the forward reaction is exothermic; increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (reverse) to absorb the extra heat.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a reversible reaction.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a reaction that can proceed in both the forward and reverse directions (products can react to re-form the reactants).

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the iron catalyst in the Haber process.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: lowers the activation energy (provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy). 1 mark: increases the rate of reaction / allows equilibrium to be reached more quickly. Do not accept: 'increases yield' or 'shifts equilibrium position'.

practice_questions.text: Ammonia manufactured by the Haber process is used to make nitrogen-containing fertilisers. Describe how ammonium nitrate fertiliser is produced from ammonia. Include the name of the intermediate compound formed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: ammonia is oxidised to form nitric acid. 1 mark: nitric acid reacts with more ammonia. 1 mark: ammonium nitrate is the product / fertiliser.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the role of auxin in phototropism?
A) Auxin moves to the illuminated side of the shoot, inhibiting growth there
B) Auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot, promoting faster elongation there
C) Auxin is destroyed by light on the shaded side, causing slower growth
D) Auxin is produced equally on both sides regardless of light direction
practice_questions.marks: B) Auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot, promoting faster elongation there [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two adaptations of a xerophyte that reduce water loss. For each adaptation, explain the mechanism by which it reduces transpiration.
practice_questions.marks:
For each adaptation (2 marks each):
• Thick, waxy cuticle — impermeable layer on leaf surface prevents direct evaporation of water through the epidermis.
• Sunken stomata — trap a pocket of humid air in the pit; reduces concentration gradient between leaf interior and external air, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.
• Rolled leaves (e.g. marram grass) — leaf curls inward enclosing humid air, reducing the water vapour gradient.
• Reduced/modified leaves (e.g. spines in cacti) — less surface area exposed to air, less evaporation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A gardener applies rooting powder to the cut end of a plant stem before placing it in soil. Explain how the auxin in rooting powder promotes root formation.
practice_questions.marks:
For each correct point:
• Rooting powder contains auxin(s)/synthetic auxins.
• Auxin promotes cell elongation in root-forming cells at the cut end of the stem.
• This stimulates the formation of adventitious roots, enabling the cutting to develop into a new, independent plant.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) Gibberellins are used commercially in the production of seedless grapes.

Describe the role of gibberellins in this process and explain why seedless grapes are commercially valuable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gibberellins applied to grape flowers stimulate fruit development without fertilisation (parthenocarpy); no seeds form because no pollen is required; fruit grows to full size; commercial value — seedless grapes are preferred by consumers (easier to eat); higher yield possible; reduced bitterness from seeds.
Secure: Gibberellins cause fruit formation without fertilisation; no seeds; commercially preferred.
Developing: Gibberellins mentioned; some connection to grape production; mechanism not fully explained.
Emerging: Gibberellins promote growth; no mention of parthenocarpy or commercial benefit.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Ethene gas is used in commercial fruit storage and ripening. Explain how ethene is used both to trigger ripening and to delay it, depending on what is required.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: To trigger ripening — unripe fruit is imported and exposed to controlled doses of ethene in ripening rooms; ethene stimulates chlorophyll breakdown, starch-to-sugar conversion and cell wall softening, producing ripe, sweet, soft fruit. To delay ripening — fruit stored in low-oxygen, low-ethene atmospheres (controlled atmosphere storage); removing ethene from the storage environment prevents the ripening signal, extending shelf life and reducing waste. Student makes explicit distinction between both applications.
Secure: Ripening rooms explained; controlled atmosphere briefly mentioned; both directions of use present.
Developing: One application fully explained; other mentioned.
Emerging: Ethene causes ripening; no explanation of controlled atmosphere or mechanism.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the effects of auxin on shoot cells and root cells, and explain how this accounts for gravitropism in a horizontally placed seedling.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Auxin accumulates on the lower side of both the horizontal shoot and root due to gravity. In the shoot, higher auxin on the lower side promotes faster elongation — the lower side grows longer and the shoot curves upward (negative gravitropism). In the root, cells are more sensitive to auxin — the higher concentration on the lower side inhibits elongation there — the upper side grows faster and the root curves downward (positive gravitropism). Student identifies the key difference in sensitivity (auxin promotes elongation in shoots, inhibits it in roots at the same concentration) and applies it correctly to both organs.
Secure: Correct direction for both root and shoot; differential sensitivity mentioned; mechanism linked to elongation.
Developing: Correct directions stated; one organ explained mechanistically.
Emerging: Shoots grow up and roots grow down; no mechanism.
[6 marks — level of response]

before.exam_tip_html: For tropism questions, always describe the mechanism: where auxin is produced, which side it accumulates on, what this does to cell elongation, and the resulting direction of bending. Simply saying ‘the plant grows towards the light’ earns no marks. For gibberellin and ethene questions, link each hormone to a specific commercial application — examiners reward precise examples (seedless grapes, banana ripening rooms, rooting powder) over vague statements about ‘promoting growth’.

practice_questions.text: Define concentration as used in chemistry calculations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The amount of solute dissolved per unit volume of solution, expressed in mol/dm³ or g/dm³.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the number of moles of hydrochloric acid in 50 cm³ of a 0.500 mol/dm³ solution.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for converting volume: 50 ÷ 1000 = 0.050 dm³. 1 mark for correct answer: n = 0.500 × 0.050 = 0.025 mol.

practice_questions.text: A solution of potassium hydroxide (KOH) has a concentration of 0.400 mol/dm³. Calculate its concentration in g/dm³. (Relative atomic masses: K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for Mr of KOH: 39 + 16 + 1 = 56. 1 mark for correct answer: 0.400 × 56 = 22.4 g/dm³.

practice_questions.text: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium carbonate solution (Na₂CO₃) is titrated against hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.200 mol/dm³. The mean titre is 30.0 cm³. The equation for the reaction is: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of the sodium carbonate solution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Step 1 — convert HCl volume: 30.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0300 dm³ (1 mark). Step 2 — moles of HCl: 0.200 × 0.0300 = 0.00600 mol (1 mark). Step 3 — mole ratio 2:1, so moles of Na₂CO₃ = 0.00600 ÷ 2 = 0.00300 mol (1 mark). Step 4 — convert Na₂CO₃ volume: 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³ (1 mark). Step 5 — concentration: 0.00300 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.120 mol/dm³ (1 mark, with unit). Step 6 — units present and steps clearly set out (1 mark). Secure: 4–5 steps correct; mole ratio applied. Developing: Steps 1–2 correct but mole ratio not applied (uses 1:1). Emerging: Correct formula stated but incorrect conversion.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would carry out a titration to find the concentration of a hydrochloric acid solution using sodium hydroxide solution of known concentration. Include the apparatus used, the role of the indicator, and how you would make the result more reliable.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Use a pipette to measure a known volume (e.g. 25.0 cm³) of HCl into a conical flask (1 mark); add a few drops of a suitable indicator, e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange (1 mark); fill a burette with NaOH solution of known concentration (1 mark); add NaOH slowly, swirling, until the indicator permanently changes colour (endpoint) (1 mark); record the titre (initial and final burette readings) (1 mark); repeat titrations to obtain concordant results (within 0.10 cm³ of each other) and calculate a mean titre (1 mark). Secure: 4–5 points with correct apparatus named. Developing: Procedure correct but reliability method missing. Emerging: Mentions burette and indicator but steps unclear.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether titration is a more reliable method than direct weighing for determining the concentration of a solution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Titration strengths — highly precise volumes measurable with burette (±0.05 cm³); colour-change endpoint can be identified reproducibly; repeat titrations allow concordant results to average out random error; suitable for very low concentrations. Direct weighing strengths — quick, no chemical reactions needed, suitable for solid solutes. Titration limitations — indicator must be chosen to match the specific reaction; endpoint detection subjective; works only for reactions that go to completion. Direct weighing limitations — does not account for impurity, water of crystallisation, or incomplete dissolution. Justified conclusion: titration is generally more reliable for acid-base concentration determination because endpoint detection gives a precise equivalence point, but direct weighing is appropriate for simpler dissolution calculations. Secure: Both methods evaluated, conclusion present but less nuanced. Developing: Titration described well, weighing comparison superficial. Emerging: Describes titration only.

practice_questions.text: An ammeter reads 0.5 A when connected in a circuit for 60 seconds. Calculate the charge that flows.
practice_questions.marks:
Q = It [1 mark for correct equation or substitution]
Q = 0.5 × 60 = 30 C [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: State what an ohmic conductor is.
practice_questions.marks: A conductor in which current is directly proportional to potential difference (at constant temperature). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A resistor has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 0.4 A flowing through it. Calculate its resistance.
practice_questions.marks:
R = V/I [1 mark for correct equation or rearrangement]
R = 12 / 0.4 = 30 Ω [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: Describe the I-V characteristics of a filament lamp and explain the shape of the graph in terms of resistance.
practice_questions.marks:
I-V graph is curved — the gradient decreases as p.d. increases [1 mark]. This means resistance increases as current increases [1 mark]. The filament heats up as more current flows [1 mark], and at higher temperatures the tungsten filament has greater resistance [1 mark].
(Allow marks in any order if points are clearly made.)

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the I-V characteristics of both a resistor and a filament lamp. Describe the method the student should use, including how the I-V graph is plotted.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full method: component in series with ammeter and variable resistor; voltmeter in parallel across component; adjust variable resistor to change p.d.; record I and V for at least 6 values; repeat readings; plot I (y-axis) vs V (x-axis); include reverse polarity by reversing connections; note to allow cooling time for filament lamp.
Secure: Correct circuit description with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel; adjusting variable resistor; plotting graph; may miss reverse polarity or cooling instruction.
Developing: Circuit partially described; mentions ammeter and voltmeter but connection direction may be wrong; graph plotting mentioned.
Emerging: General statement about measuring current and voltage without method detail.

practice_questions.text: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel to a 12 V supply. Calculate (i) the potential difference across each resistor, and (ii) the current through each resistor.
practice_questions.marks:
(i) In parallel, both resistors have the same p.d. as the supply: 12 V each. [1 mark]
(ii) Current through 6 Ω: I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A [1 mark for equation; 1 mark for answer]
Current through 3 Ω: I = 12/3 = 4 A [1 mark for answer]
Total current from supply: 2 + 4 = 6 A [1 mark]
[1 mark for consistent unit throughout]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what happens when sodium bonds with chlorine?
A) Sodium shares one electron with chlorine
B) Sodium gains one electron from chlorine
C) Sodium loses one electron to chlorine
D) Sodium and chlorine both lose one electron
practice_questions.marks: C) Sodium loses one electron to chlorine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a covalent bond.
practice_questions.marks: A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms [1 mark]. Both atoms count the shared pair as part of their own outer shell.

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'In metallic bonding, the electrons are trapped inside individual atoms.' Identify the error in this statement and give the correct description.
practice_questions.marks: Error: the electrons are not trapped — they are delocalised (free to move throughout the structure) [1 mark]. Correct description: outer electrons leave their parent atoms and form a sea of delocalised electrons that surrounds positive metal ions [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why ionic compounds can conduct electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): When dissolved, the ions are free to move through the solution and can carry electrical charge from one electrode to the other [2 marks]. When solid, the ions are fixed in the giant ionic lattice and cannot move, so charge cannot be carried [2 marks].
Secure (3): States ions are free when dissolved and not free when solid, but does not fully explain charge-carrying for both.
Developing (2): Mentions 'ions move' for one state without explaining the other.
Emerging (1): Vague answer about electricity needing something to flow.

practice_questions.text: A student draws a dot-and-cross diagram for water (H₂O). Describe the features that the examiner would expect to see in a correct diagram.
practice_questions.marks: Any three of: only outer-shell electrons shown [1]; oxygen shown with six outer electrons and two lone pairs after bonding [1]; each hydrogen shown with one electron [1]; shared pairs sit in the overlap between O and each H [1]; total of eight electrons around oxygen (including the two bonding pairs) [1]. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Magnesium oxide (MgO) has a much higher melting point than water (H₂O). Explain why, in terms of bonding and structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): MgO is an ionic compound with a giant ionic lattice structure [1]. Strong electrostatic forces between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions act in all directions [1]. A large amount of energy is required to overcome these forces, giving a high melting point [1]. Water consists of simple covalent molecules [1]. Although the O–H bonds within the molecule are strong, the intermolecular forces between water molecules are weak [1]. Little energy is needed to overcome these weak forces, so water has a low melting point [1].
Secure (3–4): Correctly explains one substance in full, other partially.
Developing (1–2): Mentions 'strong bonds' in MgO vs 'weak bonds' in water without specifying ionic vs intermolecular forces.

practice_questions.text:
Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination of movement?
A) Cerebral hemispheres
B) Medulla oblongata
C) Cerebellum
D) Spinal cord
practice_questions.marks: C) Cerebellum [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the stage of mitosis during which chromosome copies are pulled to opposite poles of the cell.
practice_questions.marks: Anaphase [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A child's height measurement falls on the 25th percentile. Explain what this tells a doctor about the child's growth.
practice_questions.marks: 25% of children of the same age are shorter than this child (or 75% are taller) [1 mark]. The child's height is within the normal range and does not immediately indicate a growth problem [1 mark]. (Accept equivalent correct interpretation.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why embryonic stem cells are considered more useful than adult stem cells for medical treatments, and describe one ethical objection to their use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent — they can differentiate into any cell type in the body, making them potentially useful for replacing any damaged or missing tissue (e.g. nerve cells after spinal injury, insulin-producing cells for diabetes). Adult stem cells are more limited in the types of cell they can become (e.g. bone marrow stem cells only produce blood cells). Ethical objection: extracting embryonic stem cells destroys the embryo, which some people consider to be taking a human life. (4 marks)
Secure: Pluripotency explained, adult stem cell limitation stated, ethical objection identified. (3 marks)
Developing: One medical use given and objection stated without full explanation. (2 marks)
Emerging: Simple statement that embryonic cells are 'more useful'. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the differences between CT scanning and PET scanning in investigating the brain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: CT uses X-rays from multiple angles to create structural images — useful for identifying tumours or bleeds. PET uses a radioactive glucose tracer to produce functional maps showing which brain regions are most active during a task — useful for studying disease or mapping functions. CT shows structure; PET shows function. (4 marks)
Secure: Both techniques described accurately with the structure vs function distinction made. (3 marks)
Developing: One technique accurately described. (2 marks)
Emerging: One simple point, e.g. 'PET uses radioactivity'. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) A student claims: 'Studying the brain is impossible without surgery.'
Using your knowledge of brain scanning, evaluate this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues clearly against the claim using CT and PET scanning as evidence. Explains what each reveals (structure vs function). Acknowledges that scanning has limitations compared to direct study (e.g. spatial resolution, radiation dose, cost). Notes that some knowledge of brain function came historically from studying people with brain injuries (case study approach). Conclusion is explicit and weighs evidence: scanning has transformed our understanding without surgery but does have limitations. (6 marks)
Secure: Both scanning techniques discussed, limitations acknowledged, justified conclusion. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Both techniques described rather than evaluated; limited conclusion. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: One scanning technique mentioned. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of energy being transferred by heating?
A) A ball rolling down a slope
B) A current flowing through a resistor making it warm
C) A stretched spring released to launch a ball
D) Sound waves from a speaker

A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from rest at a height of 8 m. Calculate the speed of the ball just before it hits the ground. Assume all gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy. Use g = 10 N/kg. Show your working.

A machine has an input energy of 2000 J and a useful output energy of 1500 J.
(a) Calculate the efficiency of the machine as a percentage. [2]
(b) State what happens to the remaining energy. [1]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Efficiency = 1500 / 2000 = 0.75 [1]; 75% [1]
(b) It is dissipated as thermal (heat) energy to the surroundings [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a falling object eventually reaches a terminal velocity when dropped from a great height in air.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Causal chain from weight > drag to equal forces to constant velocity, with correct terms throughout.
Secure: Three stages described but one causal link missing.
Developing: One or two stages described; limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple relevant statement.

Credit points:
• Object falls, initially weight greater than drag (air resistance) [1]
• Resultant force downward, so object accelerates [1]
• As speed increases, drag increases [1]
• When drag equals weight, resultant force is zero [1]
• Object continues at constant speed — terminal velocity [1]
(Max 4.)

practice_questions.text:
A spring with spring constant 200 N/m is compressed by 0.04 m.
(a) Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring. Show your working. [2]
(b) When released, the spring launches a 0.01 kg ball. Assuming all elastic potential energy converts to kinetic energy, calculate the launch speed of the ball. [3]

A student claims that it is impossible to design a machine that is 100% efficient. Evaluate this claim, explaining the physics behind energy dissipation and what factors determine how much energy is wasted.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear evaluation referencing conservation of energy and specific causes of dissipation, with a justified conclusion.
Secure: Two or more causes of dissipation with explanation; conservation of energy mentioned.
Developing: Claim supported but explanation limited to one factor.
Emerging: Simple relevant statement.

Credit points (any 6):
• The law of conservation of energy means energy cannot be destroyed [1]
• In any real machine, some energy is always dissipated as thermal energy [1]
• Causes of dissipation: friction between moving parts [1]; electrical resistance in wires [1]; sound energy emitted [1]
• Higher friction → more energy dissipated → lower efficiency [1]
• Efficiency can be improved by reducing friction (lubrication, better bearings) [1]
• Claim is correct: no real device reaches 100% efficiency [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions. In your answer, explain why different fractions condense at different levels in the column.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains crude oil is heated until vaporised; fractionating column has temperature gradient (hot at bottom, cool at top); different fractions have different boiling points due to different molecular sizes; larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces — higher boiling point — condense lower down. All four points clearly linked.
Secure: Mentions temperature gradient and boiling points; links to molecular size; may not explain intermolecular forces.
Developing: States crude oil is heated and fractions are separated; vague reference to boiling point without explanation.
Emerging: States oil is separated without explaining the mechanism.

practice_questions.text: A student burns propane (C₃H₈) in a plentiful supply of oxygen. Write a balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of propane.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct products (CO₂ and H₂O). 1 mark: correctly balanced equation: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Allow state symbols if given correctly, but not required.

practice_questions.text: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous to health. Include a description of the process by which it causes harm.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: carbon monoxide is produced by incomplete combustion (limited oxygen supply). 1 mark: it binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells. 1 mark: this prevents oxygen from being carried around the body / reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens in catalytic cracking, including: what is added, the conditions used, and the type of products formed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: large hydrocarbon molecules are vaporised and passed over a catalyst (aluminium oxide / zeolite). 1 mark: at approximately 500°C. 1 mark: products include shorter-chain alkanes AND at least one alkene (unsaturated product with C=C bond).

practice_questions.text: State one difference between an alkane and an alkene, and describe a chemical test that would allow you to distinguish between them.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: alkane is saturated (only C–C single bonds); alkene is unsaturated (contains a C=C double bond). 1 mark: add bromine water — alkene decolourises it (orange to colourless); alkane does not react (stays orange).

practice_questions.text: Burning hydrocarbon fuels releases several pollutants into the atmosphere. Evaluate the environmental impact of two of these pollutants, referring to their origin and the problems they cause.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Selects two pollutants (e.g. SO₂ and CO₂, or NOₓ and CO₂); clearly explains origin of each (SO₂ from sulfur impurities, NOₓ from high-temperature combustion of N₂ in air, CO₂ from complete combustion); describes environmental impact with precision (acid rain — lowers pH of rain, damages limestone buildings, harms aquatic life; global warming — enhanced greenhouse effect); evaluates relative severity or difficulty of mitigation; reaches a balanced, evidenced judgement.
Secure: Two pollutants identified; origin and impact for each described accurately; some comparative evaluation; conclusion present but may lack full development.
Developing: One pollutant discussed well; second pollutant mentioned but impact vague; no real evaluation or conclusion.
Emerging: Names pollutants with general environmental statements; origin not explained; no comparative judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which wire in a three-pin plug is coloured brown?
A) Earth wire
B) Neutral wire
C) Live wire
D) Fuse wire
practice_questions.marks: C) Live wire [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State why the National Grid transmits electricity at high voltage.
practice_questions.marks: High voltage means lower current [accept: to reduce current]; this reduces power wasted as heat in the cables [accept: reduces energy losses / reduces P = I²R losses]. [1 mark for correct reasoning — voltage alone is not enough without the current/loss explanation]

practice_questions.text: A toaster is rated 900 W and operates at 230 V. Calculate the current it draws.
practice_questions.marks:
P = IV → I = P/V [1 mark for correct rearrangement]
I = 900/230 = 3.9 A (to 2 s.f.) [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: A transmission cable has a resistance of 5 Ω. When a current of 200 A flows through it, calculate the power dissipated as heat.
practice_questions.marks:
P = I²R [1 mark for correct equation]
P = 200² × 5 = 40 000 × 5 [1 mark for correct substitution]
P = 200 000 W (200 kW) [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: Explain why fuses and circuit breakers are safety devices, and compare how each works.
practice_questions.marks:
Fuse: contains a thin wire in the live wire [1 mark]; if current exceeds the rated value, the wire heats up and melts, breaking the circuit [1 mark].
Circuit breaker: an automatic switch in the live wire [1 mark]; trips (opens) when current exceeds a safe level and can be reset after the fault is fixed, unlike a fuse which must be replaced [1 mark].
(Accept RCD explanation for circuit breaker.)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the National Grid distributes electricity efficiently from power stations to homes. Include reference to the role of transformers and the reason for transmitting at high voltage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation covering — electricity generated at power station; step-up transformer increases voltage (to 132 kV–400 kV) and decreases current proportionally; transmission via high-voltage cables/pylons; low current minimises power lost as heat (P = I²R, explicitly stated and linked); step-down transformers at substations progressively reduce voltage (to 33 kV → 11 kV → 230 V domestic); transformers require a.c. because only a.c. produces a changing magnetic field to induce voltage in secondary coil; conclusion that this system is more efficient than transmitting at low voltage.
Secure: Most steps covered with P = I²R explained; may miss a.c. requirement or one transformer stage.
Developing: Mentions high voltage and low current with transformers but P = I²R not explicitly applied; direction of transformer step not always correct.
Emerging: States that high voltage is used for efficiency without linking to current or I²R.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the role of progesterone in the menstrual cycle?
A) It is produced by the pituitary gland and triggers ovulation
B) It maintains the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH
C) It causes follicle maturation in the ovary
D) It stimulates the thyroid gland to produce thyroxine
practice_questions.marks: B) It maintains the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain how adrenalin prepares the body for physical activity during a fight-or-flight response. Give three specific effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three effects, each with explanation of mechanism and why it helps: e.g. heart rate increases (more oxygen/glucose delivered per minute to muscles for aerobic respiration); blood glucose rises (liver breaks down glycogen to glucose — more fuel available for muscle contraction); airways dilate (more oxygen can be inhaled per breath — increases oxygen supply to blood). Each linked causally to the survival benefit.
Secure: Three effects named with at least two mechanisms explained.
Developing: Two effects with mechanisms; one is vague.
Emerging: One or two effects named without mechanisms.
[4 marks — 1 mark per explained effect + 1 overall for logical structure]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the negative feedback mechanism that controls thyroxine levels in the blood. Name all the hormones and organs involved.
practice_questions.marks:
For each correct point:
• Hypothalamus detects low thyroxine and releases TRH.
• TRH signals pituitary gland to release TSH.
• TSH stimulates thyroid gland to produce and release thyroxine.
• High blood thyroxine inhibits hypothalamus (reducing TRH) and pituitary (reducing TSH), preventing further thyroxine increase.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) A student is given a graph showing FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone levels during the 28-day menstrual cycle. The LH surge occurs at day 14.

Explain why the LH surge occurs at around day 14 and what it causes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: As oestrogen builds up over days 1–13 (produced by the maturing follicle under FSH stimulation), high oestrogen concentration stimulates the pituitary to release a surge of LH; this surge triggers ovulation — the release of the mature egg from the follicle into the fallopian tube on approximately day 14. Student links rising oestrogen → LH surge → ovulation causally.
Secure: LH surge caused by high oestrogen; ovulation occurs as result.
Developing: LH causes ovulation; oestrogen link mentioned but not explained.
Emerging: Day 14 identified; no mechanism.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Clomifene is a fertility drug. Explain how clomifene increases the chance of ovulation in a woman who does not produce enough FSH.
practice_questions.marks:
For each correct point:
• Clomifene blocks oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus.
• The hypothalamus cannot detect oestrogen, so interprets this as low oestrogen — increases release of signals that stimulate FSH (and LH) production by the pituitary.
• Higher FSH levels stimulate follicle maturation and ovulation, increasing the chance of conception.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the nervous system and the endocrine system as methods of communication in the body. In your answer, refer to the speed, duration and specificity of each response.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Nervous system — electrical impulses travel along neurones; very fast (milliseconds); short-lived (response ends when impulse stops); highly specific (targets single cells/organs via synaptic connections); e.g. withdrawing a hand from heat. Endocrine system — hormones released into blood; slower to initiate (seconds to minutes for hormone to reach target); longer-lasting (hormone circulates until broken down); affects wider area (all cells with the target receptor); e.g. adrenalin affecting heart, liver, airways and eyes simultaneously. Student makes explicit comparison for all three criteria with examples.
Secure: All three criteria compared; at least one example per system.
Developing: Two criteria compared; one example.
Emerging: Basic contrast: one is fast, one is slow.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly explains why graphite conducts electricity?
A) It has a giant ionic lattice with free ions
B) It has delocalised electrons that can move through the layers
C) Its covalent bonds are weak and break easily
D) It has a simple molecular structure
practice_questions.marks: B) It has delocalised electrons that can move through the layers [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State why ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved in water but not when solid.
practice_questions.marks: When dissolved, the ions are free to move and carry charge [1 mark]. When solid, the ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'When water boils, the covalent bonds break.' Identify the error and give the correct explanation.
practice_questions.marks: Error: it is the weak intermolecular forces between water molecules that are overcome, not the strong covalent O–H bonds [1 mark]. The covalent bonds within the water molecules remain intact when water boils [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Compare the structure and properties of diamond and graphite, explaining how their different structures lead to their different properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Diamond — each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid tetrahedral lattice [1], making it very hard [1] and a non-conductor because all electrons are in bonds [1]. Graphite — each carbon bonds to three others in flat hexagonal layers [1], with one delocalised electron per carbon making it a conductor [1], and weak forces between layers make it soft and slippery [1].
Secure (3–4): Correctly explains one allotrope in full, other partially.
