Developing (1–2): Mentions '4 bonds' or '3 bonds' but does not link to properties.

practice_questions.text: Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) has a molecular formula and structure very different from diamond. Describe the structure of C₆₀ and suggest one potential application.
practice_questions.marks: Structure: 60 carbon atoms [1] arranged in a hollow sphere (like a football) with each carbon bonded to three others [1]. Application: any reasonable suggestion — e.g. drug delivery (the hollow cage can carry molecules), lubricants, or use in electronics [1].

practice_questions.text: 'Graphene is the most useful material discovered in the last 50 years.' Evaluate this claim, referring to the properties of graphene and the limitations of the statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Properties supporting the claim — graphene is one atom thick, extremely strong per unit mass, and conducts electricity and heat very well [1 per valid property, up to 2]. These make it valuable in electronics, composites and flexible displays [1 application]. Limitations — large-scale production is still expensive and difficult, properties in bulk differ from individual sheets, and other recently isolated materials (e.g. other 2D materials) are also significant [1 per valid limitation, up to 2]. Justified conclusion — e.g. graphene has outstanding potential but calling it definitively 'most useful' overstates current practical impact [1].
Secure (3–4): Multiple valid points, limited evaluation or conclusion.
Developing (2): Some valid properties mentioned, little evaluation.
Emerging (1): Only a single vague property.

practice_questions.text: A student carries out paper chromatography to separate a mixture of dyes. The solvent front travels 9.0 cm from the baseline. Dye A travels 6.3 cm and dye B travels 4.5 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf value of each dye. (b) A known reference dye has an Rf value of 0.70 in this solvent. Identify which dye in the mixture matches the reference.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Rf for dye A = 6.3 ÷ 9.0 = 0.70 (correctly calculated). 1 mark: Rf for dye B = 4.5 ÷ 9.0 = 0.50 (correctly calculated). 1 mark: dye A matches the reference (Rf = 0.70 = 0.70). ECF applies in part (b) if Rf values are wrong but identification is consistent with those values.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would carry out a flame test to identify the metal ions in an unknown solution. Include the steps and how you would interpret the result.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: clean a nichrome wire loop (in concentrated HCl or by burning until no colour shows). 1 mark: dip wire in the solution and hold it in the (roaring/blue) Bunsen flame. 1 mark: observe the flame colour and compare with known values (e.g. crimson = lithium, yellow = sodium, lilac = potassium).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the flame photometer is more useful than a flame test for analysing metal ions in a patient's blood sample.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: flame photometer is more sensitive — it can detect very low concentrations of ions that a manual flame test could not. 1 mark: flame photometer is quantitative — it measures the concentration of the ion, not just whether it is present; manual flame test is qualitative only.

practice_questions.text: State the test and the result for each of the following gases: (a) hydrogen, (b) carbon dioxide, (c) chlorine.
practice_questions.marks: (a) 1 mark: hold a lit splint near the gas — produces a squeaky pop. (b) 1 mark: bubble through limewater — turns milky/cloudy white. (c) 1 mark: hold damp litmus paper in the gas — turns red then bleaches white.

practice_questions.text: A solution contains an unknown metal ion. Sodium hydroxide solution is added and a white precipitate forms. The precipitate dissolves when excess NaOH is added. Identify the metal ion. Explain your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: aluminium ion (Al³⁺). 1 mark: aluminium hydroxide forms a white precipitate with NaOH, but unlike calcium hydroxide it dissolves in excess NaOH (it is amphoteric / reacts with excess alkali).

practice_questions.text: A student suspects that a white powder contains sodium ions. Describe TWO tests they could use to identify sodium ions, and state the expected result for each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes both flame test (bright yellow flame) and flame photometer (detects characteristic wavelength for sodium); gives expected result for each; notes that the flame photometer is more sensitive/quantitative.
Secure: Two tests described with correct results; does not compare sensitivity or give full detail on photometer.
Developing: Flame test described correctly; second test only vaguely described or incorrect result given.
Emerging: Only one test described; result may be incomplete.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a non-renewable energy resource?
A) Solar
B) Tidal
C) Natural gas
D) Geothermal
practice_questions.marks: C) Natural gas [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one environmental advantage and one environmental disadvantage of using wind turbines to generate electricity.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage: no carbon dioxide (or greenhouse gas) emissions during operation [1 mark]. Disadvantage: any one of — noise for nearby residents; visual impact on landscape; variable output dependent on wind speed; habitat disruption during construction [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A tidal barrage generates 4,500,000 J of energy in 900 s. Calculate the power output of the barrage. Give your answer in kilowatts.
practice_questions.marks: P = E/t [1 mark]; P = 4,500,000 ÷ 900 = 5,000 W [1 mark]; = 5 kW [1 mark — with correct unit].

practice_questions.text: Explain why fossil fuels are described as non-renewable, and explain two environmental problems caused by burning them.
practice_questions.marks: Non-renewable: formed over millions of years so cannot be replaced within a human timescale — once used, the supply is permanently reduced [1 mark]. Problem 1: burning releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and contributes to global warming / climate change [1 mark + development for link to consequence, 1 mark]. Problem 2: burning coal/oil releases sulfur dioxide which dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, damaging ecosystems and buildings [1 mark]. (Any two well-explained problems: 2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: A household uses a 3 kW electric shower for 8 minutes every day. Calculate the total energy transferred by the shower in one week (7 days). Give your answer in joules.
practice_questions.marks: Step 1: Convert power to watts — 3 kW = 3,000 W [1 mark]. Step 2: Convert time to seconds per day — 8 × 60 = 480 s [1 mark]. Step 3: Energy per day — E = Pt = 3,000 × 480 = 1,440,000 J [1 mark]. Step 4: Total for one week — 1,440,000 × 7 = 10,080,000 J [1 mark + unit mark: J]. Mastering: all steps correct with clear working, correct unit [5–6]. Secure: minor arithmetic slip but correct method [3–4]. Developing: power or time conversion correct but one major error [2]. Emerging: formula stated but substitution incorrect [1].

practice_questions.text: 'Renewable energy sources will always be preferable to fossil fuels for generating electricity.' Evaluate this statement, referring to specific energy resources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments supporting the statement: renewables produce no CO2 during operation, reducing climate change; they will not run out unlike finite fossil fuels; solar and wind have decreasing costs; tidal is highly predictable. Arguments against: many renewables are weather-dependent (solar/wind produce nothing on calm, cloudy days); fossil fuels are reliable and can respond to peak demand instantly; renewables often require large land areas or coastal locations; biofuels still release CO2 when burned. Evaluative conclusion: neither type is universally preferable — the best choice depends on location, reliability requirements and available storage infrastructure. A balanced national energy mix is typically more practical than 100% renewables without large-scale storage. Mastering: sustained, well-organised argument with named resources, specific impacts, and a justified conclusion reaching beyond 'it depends'. Secure: clear points on both sides with developed examples. Developing: relevant points but limited analysis. Emerging: simple points, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the role of the relay neurone?
A) Carries impulses from receptors to the spinal cord
B) Connects sensory and motor neurones within the CNS
C) Carries impulses from the spinal cord to muscles
D) Releases neurotransmitters into the blood
practice_questions.marks: B) Connects sensory and motor neurones within the CNS [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the function of the myelin sheath.
practice_questions.marks: It insulates the axon and speeds up the transmission of nerve impulses. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a neurotransmitter transmits a signal across a synapse.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Electrical impulse arrives at the end of the pre-synaptic neurone; neurotransmitter is released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft; it diffuses across the gap; binds to complementary receptor proteins on the post-synaptic neurone membrane; triggers a new electrical impulse in the next neurone. Correctly notes one-directional transmission. (4 marks)
Secure: Three or four correct steps, sequence clear. (3 marks)
Developing: Two correct steps, e.g. neurotransmitter released and diffuses. (2 marks)
Emerging: Simple statement that a chemical carries the signal. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
A student touches a sharp pin with her finger and immediately pulls her hand away before feeling pain.
Explain how the reflex arc produces this rapid response.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Pain receptors in the skin detect the stimulus; a sensory neurone carries an impulse to the spinal cord; a relay neurone in the spinal cord connects to a motor neurone; the motor neurone carries an impulse to the arm muscles (effector), which contract and withdraw the hand. The response bypasses the brain, so it occurs before the student consciously feels pain. (4 marks)
Secure: Correct pathway named with effector response and bypass of brain explained. (3 marks)
Developing: Correct pathway without full explanation of speed advantage. (2 marks)
Emerging: Mentions sensory and motor neurone but sequence incomplete. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with short-sightedness. Explain what causes this condition and how it is corrected.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Short-sightedness occurs when the eyeball is too long (or the cornea too curved), causing light from distant objects to be focused in front of the retina rather than on it, producing a blurred image. A concave (diverging) lens is placed in front of the eye; it spreads the light rays so that they are focused further back, on the retina. (4 marks)
Secure: Cause and correction correctly identified with mechanism for the lens type. (3 marks)
Developing: Cause stated (eyeball too long) and type of lens named without explanation of mechanism. (2 marks)
Emerging: Identifies that a concave lens is used. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and limitations of using spectacles compared with laser eye surgery to correct short-sightedness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Spectacles — non-invasive, reversible, cheap, require no recovery time; limitations include inconvenience, risk of breaking or losing, may be uncomfortable. Laser eye surgery — permanent correction by reshaping the cornea; no need for glasses; limitations include cost, surgical risk (infection, complications), not reversible, not suitable for all patients (e.g. thin corneas). A justified conclusion weighing safety vs convenience vs permanence. (6 marks)
Secure: Both options evaluated with specific points on each side and conclusion. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Both options described rather than evaluated; limited conclusion. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: One option described. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: State the volume occupied by one mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: 24 dm³ (or 24,000 cm³). Accept 24 litres.

practice_questions.text: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas (at RTP) produced when 0.25 mol of magnesium reacts completely.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying moles of H₂ = 0.25 mol (1:1 mole ratio with Mg). 1 mark for correct volume: V = 0.25 × 24 = 6.0 dm³ (with unit).

practice_questions.text: The combustion of methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the atom economy for carbon dioxide as the desired product. (Mr: CH₄ = 16, O₂ = 32, CO₂ = 44)
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for total Mr of reactants: 16 + (2 × 32) = 80. 1 mark for correct atom economy: (44/80) × 100 = 55%.

practice_questions.text: In an industrial process, 10.0 g of sulfur dioxide (SO₂, Mr = 64) is converted to sulfur trioxide (SO₃) by reaction with oxygen: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃. Only 10.5 g of SO₃ (Mr = 80) is collected. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for moles of SO₂: 10.0 ÷ 64 = 0.156 mol. 1 mark for theoretical yield of SO₃: mole ratio 1:1, so 0.156 mol × 80 = 12.5 g. 1 mark for % yield: (10.5 ÷ 12.5) × 100 = 84%.

practice_questions.text:
Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) can be manufactured by two routes:
Route A: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (Mr values: C₂H₄ = 28, H₂O = 18, C₂H₅OH = 46)
Route B: C₂H₄ + H₂O + CO₂ → C₂H₅OH + CO₂ (with CO₂ as a by-product)
Calculate the atom economy of Route A for ethanol, and explain why a chemist would prefer the route with the higher atom economy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Atom economy of Route A = (46 ÷ (28 + 18)) × 100 = (46 ÷ 46) × 100 = 100% (2 marks). Explanation: a higher atom economy means all reactant atoms end up in the desired product (1 mark), so less waste is produced, reducing environmental impact and cost of waste disposal (1 mark). Secure: Correct calculation and one explanation point. Developing: Calculation correct, explanation vague ('less waste'). Emerging: Correct formula set up but arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: A student reacts 4.0 g of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃, Mr = 100) with excess hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate (a) the theoretical volume of CO₂ produced at RTP in dm³ and (b) the percentage yield if 800 cm³ of CO₂ is actually collected.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: (a) Moles CaCO₃ = 4.0/100 = 0.040 mol (1 mark); mole ratio 1:1 so moles CO₂ = 0.040 mol (1 mark); theoretical volume = 0.040 × 24 = 0.96 dm³ (1 mark with unit). (b) Convert actual volume: 800 cm³ = 0.80 dm³ (1 mark); % yield = (0.80/0.96) × 100 = 83% (1 mark, accept 83.3%). Conclusion with unit (1 mark). Secure: (a) correct, (b) method correct but conversion of cm³ error. Developing: (a) correct, (b) does not convert cm³ to dm³. Emerging: Moles of CaCO₃ correct, further steps missing.

practice_questions.text: When a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, it becomes negatively charged. Explain why the rod becomes negative, stating which particles transfer and the direction of transfer.
practice_questions.marks:
Electrons transfer from the cloth to the polythene rod [1 mark]. The rod gains extra electrons, giving it a net negative charge [1 mark].
(Do not accept 'positive charges move' — protons cannot transfer in solid materials.)

practice_questions.text: State the rule for the forces between charged objects.
practice_questions.marks: Like charges repel; unlike (opposite) charges attract. [1 mark — must state both parts]

practice_questions.text: Describe how an electrostatic paint sprayer works, explaining why it gives an even coat with less paint waste.
practice_questions.marks: The object to be painted is given one charge (e.g. positive) [1 mark]; paint droplets are given the opposite charge (e.g. negative) [1 mark]; unlike charges attract, so paint droplets are attracted to all surfaces of the object, including difficult-to-reach areas [1 mark]; this results in an even coat and reduces waste as fewer droplets miss the target [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe the electric field pattern between two parallel plates, one positively charged and one negatively charged.
practice_questions.marks:
Field lines are parallel [1 mark]; equally spaced [1 mark]; directed from the positive plate to the negative plate / perpendicular to both plates [1 mark].
(This describes a uniform field. Accept a correct labelled sketch in place of written description.)

practice_questions.text: An aircraft is refuelled at an airport. Explain the electrostatic hazard involved and how it is managed.
practice_questions.marks: Fuel flowing through pipes causes friction, building up a static charge on the aircraft or fuel hose [1 mark]; if the charge becomes large enough, a spark could occur between the aircraft and the fuel nozzle [1 mark]; this spark could ignite fuel vapour, causing an explosion/fire [1 mark]; the aircraft is earthed (connected to ground via a conducting cable) before the fuel hose is attached, allowing charge to flow safely to earth and preventing spark formation [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of static electricity in industry. In your answer, refer to both useful applications and hazards, and reach a conclusion about whether the benefits outweigh the risks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with at least two specific applications (e.g. electrostatic paint spraying — even coat, less waste; electrostatic precipitators — reduce air pollution from chimneys; inkjet printers — precise droplet control) and at least two hazards (aircraft refuelling — spark risk; grain silos — dust explosion; operating theatres — damage to equipment); each point explained mechanistically (charge build-up → spark → ignition for hazards; attraction/repulsion principle for applications); justified conclusion stating benefits outweigh risks when proper earthing controls are in place.
Secure: Two applications and two hazards with some mechanistic explanation; conclusion present but may not be fully justified.
Developing: One or two applications or hazards identified; limited explanation of mechanisms; conclusion absent or unsupported.
Emerging: General statements about static electricity being useful or dangerous without specific examples or explanations.

practice_questions.text:
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
(Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
practice_questions.marks: Mr = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) [1 mark] = 100 [1 mark]. No unit needed for Mr.

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) Calculate the number of moles in 8.0 g of sulfur dioxide (SO₂).
(Relative atomic masses: S = 32, O = 16)
practice_questions.marks: Mr of SO₂ = 32 + (2 × 16) = 64 [1 mark for Mr]. Moles = 8.0 ÷ 64 = 0.125 mol [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
In an industrial process, hydrogen and nitrogen react to form ammonia:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
Calculate the mass of ammonia that can be produced from 6.0 g of hydrogen gas.
(Relative atomic masses: H = 1, N = 14)
practice_questions.marks: Mr of H₂ = 2; moles of H₂ = 6.0 ÷ 2 = 3.0 mol [1 mark]. Ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2, so moles of NH₃ = 3.0 × (2/3) = 2.0 mol [1 mark]. Mr of NH₃ = 14 + 3 = 17; mass = 2.0 × 17 = 34 g [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student carries out a reaction and obtains 18.4 g of product. The theoretical yield is 23.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks: Percentage yield = (18.4 ÷ 23.0) × 100 [1 mark] = 80% [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by atom economy and why a high atom economy is desirable in industrial chemical processes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): Atom economy is the proportion of the mass of reactants that ends up in the desired product [1 mark], calculated as (Mr of the desired product ÷ Mr of all reactants) × 100 [1 mark]. High atom economy means less waste is produced [1 mark], which is more cost-effective (less raw material wasted) and more sustainable/environmentally friendly [1 mark].
Secure (2–3): Correct definition and one benefit.
Developing (1): States it involves products and reactants without a correct definition.

practice_questions.text:
In the reaction: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
Calculate the atom economy for producing calcium oxide (CaO).
(Relative atomic masses: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
practice_questions.marks: Step 1 — Mr of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3×16) = 100 [1 mark]. Step 2 — CaCO₃ is the only reactant, so the total Mr of the reactants is also 100 [1 mark]. Step 3 — Mr of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 [1 mark]. Step 4 — check with the other product: Mr of CO₂ = 12 + (2×16) = 44, and 56 + 44 = 100, so mass is conserved [1 mark]. Step 5 — Atom economy = (56 ÷ 100) × 100 = 56% [1 mark]. Step 6 — Interpretation: 44% of the starting mass becomes CO₂ waste; this is a moderate atom economy and the CO₂ by-product has implications for carbon emissions in industrial lime production [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what happens to the atomic number and mass number during beta-minus decay?
A) Atomic number increases by 1; mass number increases by 1
B) Atomic number increases by 1; mass number stays the same
C) Atomic number decreases by 1; mass number stays the same
D) Atomic number stays the same; mass number decreases by 1
practice_questions.marks: B) Atomic number increases by 1; mass number stays the same [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the unit of radioactive activity.
practice_questions.marks: Becquerel / Bq [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A radioactive nucleus undergoes alpha decay. The parent nucleus has mass number 238 and atomic number 92. Write a balanced nuclear equation for this decay, identifying the daughter nucleus.
practice_questions.marks:
Daughter mass number = 238 − 4 = 234 [1 mark]; daughter atomic number = 92 − 2 = 90 [1 mark]; correct equation written with both numbers in correct positions and alpha particle shown as \(^4_2\text{He}\) [1 mark]. Accept any correctly written nuclear equation format.

Note: atomic number 90 = thorium (Th). Equation: \(^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^4_2\text{He}\)

practice_questions.text: A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 3200 Bq. The half-life of the isotope is 8 days. Calculate the activity of the sample after 32 days. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Number of half-lives = 32 ÷ 8 = 4 [1 mark]; correct application of \((\tfrac{1}{2})^4 = \tfrac{1}{16}\) or repeated halving: 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200 [1 mark]; final answer: 200 Bq [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'After three half-lives, three-quarters of the original sample has decayed.' Explain whether this statement is correct, using a calculation to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: The statement is incorrect [1 mark]; after three half-lives the fraction remaining is \((\tfrac{1}{2})^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}\) [1 mark]; therefore the fraction that has decayed is \(1 - \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{7}{8}\) [1 mark]; the student has confused three half-lives (×3) with the fraction remaining, which halves exponentially each half-life rather than decreasing by a fixed fraction each time [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 30 years. An archaeological sample is found to contain 12.5% of the original amount of the isotope. Calculate how many years ago the sample was formed. Show all working.

Explain why it is not possible to predict exactly when a single nucleus in the sample will decay.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6): Correctly identifies that 12.5% = \(\tfrac{1}{8}\) of the original [1 mark]; recognises this corresponds to 3 half-lives because \((\tfrac{1}{2})^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}\) [1 mark]; time elapsed = 3 × 30 = 90 years [1 mark]; states units clearly; explains that radioactive decay is a random process [1 mark]; so it is impossible to predict when any individual nucleus will decay [1 mark]; but for very large numbers of nuclei, statistical behaviour is predictable, hence half-life is meaningful [1 mark].

Secure (4–5): Correct calculation and partial explanation of randomness.
Developing (2–3): Correct number of half-lives or partial calculation with some relevant physics.
Emerging (0–1): Isolated correct step or relevant statement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following base pairs is found in DNA?
A) Adenine with guanine
B) Cytosine with adenine
C) Thymine with adenine
D) Guanine with uracil
practice_questions.marks: C) Thymine with adenine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'allele'.
practice_questions.marks: A different version of the same gene [1 mark]. (Accept: one of two or more alternative forms of a gene.)

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) A man with blood group A (genotype I^A I^O) and a woman with blood group B (genotype I^B I^O) have children.
Using a Punnett square, determine the possible blood groups of their children and the probability of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Correct Punnett square with gametes I^A / I^O and I^B / I^O [1 mark]
Offspring genotypes: I^A I^B (group AB), I^A I^O (group A), I^B I^O (group B), I^O I^O (group O) [1 mark]
Each blood group has a 1 in 4 (25%) probability [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain what codominance means and use ABO blood groups to illustrate your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Codominance is when both alleles are expressed equally in the phenotype of the heterozygote — neither is dominant over the other. In ABO blood groups, I^A and I^B are codominant: a person with genotype I^A I^B expresses both A and B antigens on their red blood cells, giving blood group AB. (4 marks)
Secure: Correct definition of codominance and correct example with genotype and phenotype. (3 marks)
Developing: Correct example of AB genotype but definition of codominance unclear or incomplete. (2 marks)
Emerging: States that AB has both A and B antigens but no explanation of codominance. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the process of transcription during protein synthesis.
practice_questions.marks: RNA polymerase binds to the gene on the DNA [1 mark]; reads the template strand of DNA and assembles a complementary mRNA strand using RNA bases (A pairs with U; C pairs with G) [1 mark]; the mRNA strand leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores to reach the ribosome [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Gregor Mendel proposed the principles of inheritance from his pea plant experiments, but his ideas were not accepted for many years after publication.
Evaluate reasons why Mendel's work was initially ignored, and why it was later accepted.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues both sides. Reasons for initial rejection: Mendel was an obscure monk with no formal scientific position; his work was published in a minor journal; the mathematical approach was unfamiliar to biologists of the time; there was no known mechanism to explain how 'factors' were passed on. Reasons for later acceptance: discovery of chromosomes and meiosis provided the physical mechanism for Mendel's ratios; scientists re-reading his paper in the early 1900s (de Vries, Correns, von Tschermak) independently reproduced his results; the chromosome theory unified his ratios with observable cell biology. Balanced conclusion with explicit criteria. (6 marks)
Secure: Both sides argued with specific points; conclusion present. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Points listed rather than evaluated; limited weighing of evidence. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: One side described. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a longitudinal wave?
A) Oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
B) Oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer
C) The wave can only travel through a vacuum
D) The wave always has a higher speed than transverse waves
practice_questions.marks: B) Oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between the amplitude and the wavelength of a wave.
practice_questions.marks: Amplitude: maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position [1 mark]. Wavelength: distance between two successive equivalent points on a wave, e.g. crest to crest [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A water wave has a frequency of 2.5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.40 m. Calculate the speed of the wave.
practice_questions.marks: v = fλ = 2.5 × 0.40 [1 mark] = 1.0 m/s [1 mark — with unit].

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the speed, frequency and wavelength of a wave when it crosses from a less dense medium into a denser medium.
practice_questions.marks: Speed decreases [1 mark]; frequency remains the same / unchanged [1 mark]; wavelength decreases (because v = fλ and f is constant, if v decreases, λ must also decrease) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the speed of sound in a metal rod. She strikes one end of a 3.0 m rod with a hammer. A detector at the other end records the sound pulse arriving 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ s later. Calculate the speed of sound in the rod and explain one advantage of this method over using a ripple tank to measure wave speed.
practice_questions.marks: v = x/t [1 mark]; v = 3.0 ÷ (8.0 × 10⁻⁴) [1 mark]; = 3,750 m/s [1 mark + unit]. Advantage: any one well explained, e.g. the rod gives a sharp, well-defined pulse that is easy to detect precisely with a data logger, whereas water wave measurements are affected by surface tension and depth variations making accurate wavelength measurement harder [1 mark for stated advantage, 1 mark for explanation]. Mastering: clear multi-step working and a developed comparison [5–6]. Secure: correct numerical answer with a stated advantage [3–4]. Developing: speed calculation attempted with one step correct [2]. Emerging: v = x/t stated [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain how seismic P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the internal structure of the Earth.
practice_questions.marks: P-waves are longitudinal and travel through both solids and liquids [1 mark]. S-waves are transverse and can only travel through solids [1 mark]. S-waves are not detected on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake, indicating the outer core is liquid [1 mark]. P-waves are detected but with a change in direction (refraction) at the boundary between the mantle and core, indicating a change in material [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by homeostasis.
practice_questions.marks: The maintenance of a stable internal environment (in response to internal and external changes). Accept: regulation of internal conditions to maintain optimum conditions for enzyme activity / cell function.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the body responds when core temperature rises above 37°C. Refer to blood vessels, sweat glands and hair follicles in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly names vasodilation (arterioles widen) and links to increased blood flow to skin surface and heat loss by radiation; explains sweat glands secrete more sweat and evaporation removes latent heat; states hair follicle muscles relax so hairs lie flat, reducing insulating air layer; all three effectors linked to cooling outcome.
Secure: Three of the four points above, all with correct mechanism.
Developing: Two correct mechanisms with partial explanation of the outcome.
Emerging: One correct mechanism or outcome only.

practice_questions.text: A student says that vasodilation means blood vessels move towards the skin. Explain why this is incorrect, and describe what vasodilation actually involves.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Blood vessels do not move; they are fixed structures in the dermis. 1 mark: Vasodilation is the widening (dilation) of the arterioles supplying the skin capillaries, increasing blood flow to the skin surface.

practice_questions.text: Compare Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes. In your answer, refer to the cause, the role of insulin, and the treatment for each type.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly contrasts cause (autoimmune destruction of beta cells vs. insulin resistance in cells); insulin status (little/none produced in T1 vs. produced but cells unresponsive in T2); treatment (insulin injections for T1 vs. diet/exercise/medication for T2); appropriate link between obesity and T2 risk.
Secure: Four distinct points across the three areas with mostly correct detail.
Developing: Two or three correct points but with gaps or minor errors in one area.
Emerging: One correct point about either type.

practice_questions.text: A patient has a fasting blood glucose concentration of 8.9 mmol/L (normal range: 3.9–5.5 mmol/L). Explain how the body would normally respond to a rise in blood glucose, naming the organ and hormone involved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The pancreas detects the rise in blood glucose. 1 mark: The pancreas secretes insulin. 1 mark: Insulin causes cells to take up glucose from the blood / stimulates the liver to convert glucose to glycogen, lowering blood glucose back to the set point.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of BMI as a measure of health risk for Type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains what BMI measures and its calculation; correctly identifies the obese threshold (above 30); discusses strengths (simple, non-invasive, widely used, correlates with excess adiposity); discusses limitations (doesn’t distinguish fat from muscle mass, doesn’t indicate fat distribution — waist-to-hip ratio better for this; doesn’t account for ethnicity differences in risk); reaches a justified conclusion that BMI is a useful screening tool but not a complete measure.
Secure: Covers at least two strengths and two limitations with some evaluative reasoning and a conclusion.
Developing: Identifies one strength and one limitation with limited evaluation.
Emerging: Describes what BMI is with little or no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the concentration of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere increased from almost zero to approximately 21% over billions of years.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: early photosynthetic organisms (e.g. algae/cyanobacteria) evolved in the oceans. 1 mark: they used CO₂ and released oxygen as a waste product of photosynthesis. 1 mark: over hundreds of millions of years, oxygen gradually accumulated in the atmosphere as these organisms spread.

practice_questions.text: Explain the greenhouse effect. In your answer, explain the role of greenhouse gases and why the greenhouse effect is important for life on Earth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the Sun emits short-wavelength (visible) radiation that passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface; the surface emits infrared (long-wavelength) radiation; greenhouse gases absorb this infrared and re-emit in all directions including back towards Earth; this raises surface temperature above what it would otherwise be; without this effect temperatures would be too low for life.
Secure: Four of the five points above; may lack the sequence of wavelengths or the ‘essential for life’ conclusion.
Developing: States greenhouse gases trap heat; some reference to infrared radiation; misses the solar radiation sequence.
Emerging: States gases trap heat with no mechanism.

practice_questions.text: State two human activities that have increased the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. For each activity, explain how it releases carbon dioxide.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per activity named + 1 mark per explanation. Burning fossil fuels: carbon stored as fossil fuels is oxidised to CO₂ during combustion. Deforestation: trees that absorb CO₂ during photosynthesis are removed; burning or decomposition of felled trees also releases CO₂. Other accepted: cement production (heating limestone releases CO₂). Two activities with two mechanisms required for full marks.

practice_questions.text: State the approximate percentage of nitrogen and oxygen in today's atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: nitrogen approximately 78% AND oxygen approximately 21% (both required for the mark).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the scientific evidence that human activities are causing global warming and climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes multiple independent lines of evidence (rising average temperatures; retreating glaciers; rising sea levels; correlation between CO₂ concentration and temperature over time; species range shifts); links each to greenhouse gas increase from human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture); acknowledges natural climate variation exists but explains why the current rate of change is unprecedented and attributed to human activity; provides a sustained, balanced judgement.
Secure: At least three lines of evidence; human activity linked to greenhouse gases; some reference to natural variation; conclusion present.
Developing: One or two pieces of evidence; limited mechanistic link to greenhouse effect; conclusion weak or missing.
Emerging: States humans cause global warming without evidence or mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain why scientists believe the early atmosphere of Earth was similar to the current atmospheres of Venus and Mars.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Venus and Mars have atmospheres dominated by carbon dioxide (with little oxygen). 1 mark: this matches the model of Earth's early atmosphere (mainly CO₂, no photosynthesis yet), so they provide evidence / a modern-day analogue for what Earth's early atmosphere was like.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following metals can be extracted from its ore by reduction with carbon?
A) Potassium
B) Aluminium
C) Iron
D) Sodium
practice_questions.marks: C) Iron [1 mark]. Iron is below carbon in the reactivity series, so it can be reduced by carbon. Potassium, aluminium and sodium are all above carbon and require electrolysis.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'displacement reaction' in the context of metals.
practice_questions.marks: A reaction where a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a solution of the less reactive metal's compound [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Zinc is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Write a word equation for the reaction and explain, in terms of electrons, which substance is oxidised and which is reduced.
practice_questions.marks: Word equation: zinc + copper(II) sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper [1 mark]. Zinc atoms lose electrons to become Zn²⁺ ions — zinc is oxidised [1 mark]. Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons to become copper atoms — copper(II) ions are reduced [1 mark]. Credit reference to OIL RIG [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why alloys are generally harder than the pure metals from which they are made.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): In a pure metal, atoms are the same size and arranged in a regular lattice [1]. Layers of atoms can slide over each other when a force is applied, making the metal soft and malleable [1]. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes are present [1]. These distort the regular lattice structure, so layers cannot slide over each other as easily, making the alloy harder and stronger [1].
Secure (2–3): Correct idea about different sizes but doesn't fully link to layer movement.
Developing (1): States 'different atoms are present' without linking to hardness mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Explain why aluminium is more expensive to extract than iron, despite being a more common element in the Earth's crust.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): Aluminium is above carbon in the reactivity series [1], so it cannot be extracted by reduction with carbon [1]. Instead, electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide is required [1]. Electrolysis uses large amounts of electrical energy, making the process much more expensive than reducing iron ore with carbon in a blast furnace [1].
Secure (2–3): Mentions electrolysis and expense without fully explaining why carbon cannot be used.
Developing (1): States 'electrolysis needed' without scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe what electroplating is and explain the process, including the roles of the cathode, anode and electrolyte.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Electroplating is the process of depositing a thin layer of metal onto an object using electrolysis [1]. The object to be plated is made the cathode (negative electrode) [1]. The plating metal is made the anode (positive electrode) [1]. Both are placed in a solution (electrolyte) containing ions of the plating metal [1]. Metal ions from the solution are reduced at the cathode and deposited as a metal layer [1]. The anode dissolves to replenish the metal ions in solution [1].
Secure (3–4): Correct role of cathode and anode, electrolyte mentioned, but ion replenishment or reduction step missing.
Developing (1–2): Identifies cathode/anode roles loosely without explaining ion movement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes an induced magnet?
A) It produces its own permanent magnetic field
B) It becomes magnetic only when placed in an external field and is always attracted to the permanent magnet
C) It repels permanent magnets
D) It generates a field from an electric current
practice_questions.marks: B) It becomes magnetic only when placed in an external field and is always attracted to the permanent magnet [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the three factors that affect the strength of a solenoid's magnetic field.
practice_questions.marks: Any three of: increasing the current [1 mark]; increasing the number of turns (per unit length) [1 mark]; adding or using a (soft iron) core [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A wire of length 0.20 m carries a current of 5 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.8 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
practice_questions.marks:
F = BIl [1 mark for correct equation or substitution]
F = 0.8 × 5 × 0.20 = 0.80 N [1 mark for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain how Fleming's left-hand rule is used to determine the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
practice_questions.marks: Hold the left hand with thumb, index finger and middle finger mutually at right angles [1 mark]; the index finger points in the direction of the magnetic field (north to south) [1 mark]; the middle finger points in the direction of conventional current [1 mark]; the thumb points in the direction of the force (thrust/motion) on the wire [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain the role of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor and why it is needed for continuous rotation.
practice_questions.marks: After the coil rotates 180°, the sides of the coil that were pushed up and down swap positions [1 mark]; without the commutator, the motor-effect force would act in the opposite direction and the coil would reverse direction/stop [1 mark]; the split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half-turn [1 mark]; this ensures the force always acts in the same rotational direction, maintaining continuous rotation [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe the differences between a permanent magnet and an electromagnet, and evaluate two situations in which each type is preferable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of both (permanent magnet — always magnetised, fixed poles, no energy input needed; electromagnet — requires current, switchable, strength adjustable); at least two well-chosen evaluative comparisons (e.g. permanent magnet preferred in a fridge door — no power needed, always on; electromagnet preferred in scrapyard crane — can release load on demand; permanent magnet in a compass — reliable without power; electromagnet in MRI — precise controllable strength); balanced conclusion justified by the criteria of switchability and strength control.
Secure: Accurate description of both types; two comparisons made with some evaluative comment; conclusion present.
Developing: Differences noted (one type needs current, one doesn't); one comparison; minimal evaluation.
Emerging: States one or two differences without evaluative comment or application.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes a step-up transformer?
A) It has fewer turns on the secondary coil and increases voltage
B) It has more turns on the secondary coil and decreases voltage
C) It has more turns on the secondary coil and increases voltage
D) It has fewer turns on the primary coil and decreases voltage
practice_questions.marks: C) It has more turns on the secondary coil and increases voltage [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the equation linking the moment of a force to the applied force and the distance from the pivot.
practice_questions.marks: Moment (N m) = force (N) × perpendicular distance from pivot (m) / M = F × d [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A transformer has a primary voltage of 400 V and a secondary voltage of 20 V. The primary coil has 2000 turns. Calculate the number of turns in the secondary coil.
practice_questions.marks: Use \(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\) → \(N_s = N_p \times \frac{V_s}{V_p} = 2000 \times \frac{20}{400}\) [1 mark]; \(N_s = 100\) turns [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A transformer operates with 100% efficiency. The primary coil is connected to a 12,000 V AC supply and carries a current of 5 A. The secondary coil delivers a voltage of 240 V. Calculate the current in the secondary coil. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks: Use \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s\) [1 mark]; \(I_s = \frac{V_p \times I_p}{V_s} = \frac{12000 \times 5}{240}\) [1 mark]; \(I_s = 250\) A [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain why electrical energy in the National Grid is transmitted at very high voltages rather than at the lower voltages generated by power stations.
practice_questions.marks: Transmission cables have electrical resistance [1 mark]; power dissipated as heat in cables = \(I^2 R\) [1 mark]; transmitting at high voltage means current is low (using \(P = VI\) or power equation) [1 mark]; low current greatly reduces \(I^2 R\) heat losses, making transmission more efficient [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates a balanced beam pivoted at its centre. A 60 N weight hangs 0.30 m to the left of the pivot. A second weight hangs 0.20 m to the right of the pivot, and a third weight of 10 N hangs 0.60 m to the right of the pivot.

(a) Calculate the anti-clockwise moment produced by the 60 N weight.
(b) Calculate the size of the second weight needed to keep the beam balanced. Show your working clearly.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6): (a) Anti-clockwise moment = 60 × 0.30 = 18 N m [1 mark]; (b) Total clockwise moment must equal 18 N m [1 mark]; moment from 10 N weight = 10 × 0.60 = 6 N m [1 mark]; remaining clockwise moment needed = 18 − 6 = 12 N m [1 mark]; second weight = 12 ÷ 0.20 = 60 N [1 mark]; units and clear layout [1 mark].

Secure (4–5): Correct strategy with one arithmetic or substitution error.
Developing (2–3): Correct anti-clockwise moment calculated, partial progress on part (b).
Emerging (0–1): Moment equation stated or one isolated correct multiplication.

practice_questions.text:
Which scientist, working alongside Charles Darwin, independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
A) Gregor Mendel
B) Richard Leakey
C) Alfred Wallace
D) Carl Woese
practice_questions.marks: C) Alfred Wallace [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) State the name of the enzyme used to join the sticky ends of DNA fragments together during genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks: Ligase [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A strain of bacteria has become resistant to an antibiotic.
Explain how antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Random mutation(s) produce variation in the bacterial population; some bacteria have a mutation that gives resistance to the antibiotic. When the antibiotic is applied, susceptible bacteria die but the resistant ones survive and reproduce rapidly. The resistant bacteria pass on the resistance allele to offspring; over many generations the resistant strain becomes dominant in the population. (4 marks)
Secure: Mutation leads to variation; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; allele frequency increases. (3 marks)
Developing: States that resistant bacteria survive but does not explain the role of mutation or allele inheritance. (2 marks)
Emerging: Simple statement that bacteria 'get used to' the antibiotic. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Describe the evidence for human evolution provided by the fossils of Ardi and Lucy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Ardi (Ardipithecus ramidus, ~4.4 mya) is one of the earliest known hominids; features include a mix of upright walking and tree-climbing adaptations. Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis, ~3.2 mya) shows clear bipedalism (upright walking) while retaining a small, ape-like braincase — suggesting bipedalism evolved before large brain size. Comparing the two shows a progression towards more human-like characteristics over time. (4 marks)
Secure: Both fossils named with age and one feature each as evidence of evolution towards modern humans. (3 marks)
Developing: One fossil described accurately with relevant evidence. (2 marks)
Emerging: Mentions fossil as evidence without specific detail. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the process by which a gene from one organism can be inserted into a bacterial cell using genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Restriction enzyme used to cut desired gene from donor DNA at specific base sequences, producing sticky ends; same restriction enzyme cuts the bacterial plasmid (vector); the gene is inserted into the plasmid; ligase joins the complementary sticky ends, forming a recombinant plasmid; recombinant plasmid introduced into a host bacterium; bacterium replicates and expresses the new gene, producing the desired protein. (6 marks)
Secure: All main steps present but one detail missing (e.g. sticky ends not mentioned). (4–5 marks)
Developing: Restriction enzyme and ligase named; basic sequence of steps correct. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: Mentions cutting a gene from DNA and putting it into a bacterium. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
'Selective breeding is more beneficial to humans than genetic engineering.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For selective breeding: proven track record over thousands of years (crops, livestock, pets); no laboratory technology needed; more acceptable to the public and some religious groups; produces many generations of offspring. Against: reduces genetic variation (inbreeding risk); slow process (many generations); cannot introduce traits from unrelated species. For genetic engineering: faster, more precise, can insert any gene including from different kingdoms (e.g. Bt crops, insulin-producing bacteria); Against: public and ethical concerns about 'playing with nature'; potential ecological effects of GM crops; expensive. Conclusion states criteria for judgement (e.g. speed, safety, ethics) and makes an explicit decision. (6 marks)
Secure: Both sides evaluated with specific examples; conclusion present but criteria less explicit. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Both methods described but not properly evaluated; limited conclusion. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: One method described. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes an alkene?
A) A saturated hydrocarbon with only single bonds
B) An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing at least one C=C double bond
C) A hydrocarbon that contains oxygen atoms
D) A polymer made from ethene monomers
State the result of the bromine water test when propene is added, and explain why this result occurs.
practice_questions.marks: Orange/brown solution decolourises to colourless [1]. Bromine adds across the C=C double bond in propene (addition reaction), so bromine is used up [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe the conditions needed for the fermentation of glucose to produce ethanol.
practice_questions.marks:
Yeast present [1]; anaerobic conditions (absence of oxygen) [1]; warm temperature / optimum around 25–35 °C [1].
(Accept any three distinct correct conditions.)

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Compare addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. In your answer, refer to the types of monomers required and the products formed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear comparison of both monomer type and products for each process.
Secure: Both processes addressed but one comparison point underdeveloped.
Developing: One process described correctly; comparison limited.
Emerging: Vague or single relevant point.

Credit points:
• Addition: monomers contain a C=C double bond [1]; only one product (the polymer) [1]
• Condensation: monomers have two functional groups (e.g. diol + dicarboxylic acid) [1]; small molecule released at each join, usually water [1]

practice_questions.text:
A student burns different alcohols in a core practical to compare their energy output. The student measures the mass of water heated, the temperature rise, and the mass of alcohol burned.
(a) Give one variable the student must control to make the comparison valid. [1]
(b) The student burns 0.50 g of ethanol and heats 200 g of water from 20.0 °C to 36.5 °C. Calculate the energy released in joules. Use Q = mcΔT, where c = 4.18 J/g°C. Show your working. [2]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Any one of: distance between flame and calorimeter; volume/mass of water; same calorimeter material; same draught conditions [1]
(b) ΔT = 36.5 − 20.0 = 16.5 °C [1]; Q = 200 × 4.18 × 16.5 = 13 794 J (accept 13 800 J or 13.8 kJ) [1]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of biodegradable plastics as a replacement for traditional non-biodegradable polymers. Consider both the advantages and disadvantages in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with advantages and disadvantages, concluding with a justified judgement. Uses specific examples.
Secure: At least two advantages and one disadvantage (or vice versa) with clear explanation.
Developing: One side of the argument developed; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Simple statements without explanation.

Credit points (any 6 from):
• Non-biodegradable polymers persist in landfill/oceans for centuries [1]
• Biodegradable plastics decompose, reducing landfill waste [1]
• Made from renewable sources (plant starch, sugars) [1]
• Currently more expensive to produce than traditional plastics [1]
• May have lower mechanical strength / not suitable for all applications [1]
• Decomposition may release CO₂, contributing to greenhouse effect [1]
• Recycling infrastructure also reduces plastic waste (alternative solution) [1]
• Justified conclusion weighing advantages against disadvantages [1]

practice_questions.text: State the role of the Bowman's capsule in the nephron.
practice_questions.marks: It surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate that is forced out of the blood under high pressure during ultrafiltration.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a healthy person's urine does not contain glucose, even though glucose is present in the filtrate after ultrafiltration.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Glucose is present in the filtrate after ultrafiltration in the glomerulus. 1 mark: All glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate in the nephron tubule by active transport. 1 mark: Active transport requires energy (from respiration) and moves glucose against the concentration gradient back into the surrounding capillaries.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A student exercises vigorously on a hot day and does not drink any water. Explain how their kidneys respond to maintain water balance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States blood water potential decreases / blood becomes more concentrated; hypothalamus detects this and releases more ADH; ADH increases permeability of collecting duct to water; more water is reabsorbed by osmosis into capillaries; produces smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
Secure: Four of the five points above with correct causal links.
Developing: Correctly identifies role of ADH and either collecting duct or the concentration of urine, but misses one causal step.
Emerging: States urine becomes more concentrated without explaining the mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a dialysis machine removes urea from the blood. Include the role of the partially permeable membrane and the dialysis fluid in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Blood flows on one side of a partially permeable membrane; dialysis fluid flows on the other side; urea diffuses from the blood (high concentration) across the membrane into the dialysis fluid (low concentration) down a concentration gradient; dialysis fluid contains glucose and mineral ions at the correct body concentrations so these are not lost; process is repeated over several hours.
Secure: Mentions membrane, concentration gradient for urea, and correct composition of dialysis fluid.
Developing: Describes diffusion across a membrane but does not explain why glucose is not lost.
Emerging: States blood is filtered with partial detail.

practice_questions.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of dialysis and kidney transplant as treatments for kidney failure.
practice_questions.marks: Any four comparative points, one mark each. Dialysis: widely available, no surgery required; BUT time-consuming (several times a week), restricts lifestyle/diet, does not cure kidney failure. Transplant: restores near-normal kidney function, better long-term quality of life; BUT requires matched donor (limited availability), major surgery risk, lifelong immunosuppressant drugs increase infection risk.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of a kidney transplant as a treatment for kidney failure. In your answer, consider effectiveness, risks, and the ethical issues surrounding organ donation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses effectiveness (restores full kidney function, avoids dialysis burden); risks (surgical complications, organ rejection, lifelong immunosuppression, increased infection risk); ethical points (scarcity of donors, opt-in vs. opt-out donation systems, living vs. deceased donors, equity of allocation); reaches a justified overall judgement weighing these factors.
Secure: Covers effectiveness, at least two risks and one ethical point with some evaluative reasoning and a conclusion.
Developing: Identifies some risks and benefits but limited ethical engagement; partial conclusion.
Emerging: Describes transplant with few comparative points.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly lists electromagnetic waves in order of increasing frequency?
A) Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio
B) Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
C) Radio, infrared, microwaves, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
D) Gamma rays, ultraviolet, X-rays, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio
practice_questions.marks: B) Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two uses of infrared radiation and one danger of excessive infrared exposure.
practice_questions.marks: Any two uses from: thermal imaging / remote controls / optical fibre communication / cooking (grill, toaster) / security systems [1 mark each, max 2]. Danger: skin burns [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student shines a ray of light from air into a rectangular glass block at an angle of incidence of 40°. Describe, in terms of the normal, what happens to the ray at the air–glass boundary.
practice_questions.marks: The ray bends towards the normal / the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence [1 mark]; because light slows down when it enters the denser glass [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why ultraviolet radiation is more dangerous to human health than visible light, but less dangerous than gamma rays.
practice_questions.marks: UV has higher frequency than visible light [1 mark], so each photon carries more energy and can damage surface skin cells and eyes, increasing the risk of skin cancer [1 mark]. Gamma rays have even higher frequency [1 mark], so they are highly ionising and penetrate deep into body tissue, causing cell mutation and potentially cancer [1 mark]. (Accept any four logically sequenced points linking frequency to energy to biological damage.)

practice_questions.text: A student investigates refraction using a rectangular glass block. She measures the angle of incidence and angle of refraction at several different angles. Describe how she should conduct the investigation, including how she would collect valid data and identify any sources of error.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): describes placing block on paper, drawing around it, directing single ray at several angles, marking entry and exit points, removing block and reconstructing full ray path, measuring angles from the normal using protractor; identifies control variables (same block, same distance from source); states how to reduce parallax error (eye level with surface when marking exit point); notes random error from ray width. Secure (3–4): correct sequence of method steps, mentions normal and angle measurement; may omit controls or error analysis. Developing (2): some correct method steps but incomplete. Emerging (1): mentions glass block and ray of light.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) All bodies emit electromagnetic radiation. Explain how the temperature of a body affects the intensity and wavelength of radiation it emits, and use this to explain why the Earth's temperature remains approximately constant.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): explains that hotter bodies emit more intense radiation and at shorter peak wavelength; Earth absorbs solar radiation and emits infrared; for constant temperature, power absorbed must equal power emitted; greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit in all directions, reducing net loss; if power in exceeds power out, Earth warms until new balance reached. Secure (3–4): covers emission–absorption balance and greenhouse effect with some development. Developing (2): relevant points on emission and temperature but limited explanation of Earth's balance. Emerging (1): states that hotter objects emit more radiation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by electromagnetic induction.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The production of a voltage (or EMF / electromotive force) in a conductor when it experiences a changing magnetic field.

practice_questions.text: A student moves a bar magnet towards a coil of wire connected to a galvanometer. The galvanometer needle deflects. Identify the effect being demonstrated and explain one way the student could make the needle deflect more.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the generator effect / electromagnetic induction. 1 mark for a correct method with explanation: e.g. move the magnet faster — the conductor cuts field lines more quickly, inducing a larger EMF / use a stronger magnet — the magnetic field is more intense, increasing the rate of change of flux.

practice_questions.text: A transformer has a primary voltage of 400 V and a primary coil of 800 turns. The secondary coil has 200 turns. Calculate the secondary voltage.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct substitution: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns → 400/Vs = 800/200. 1 mark for correct answer: Vs = 100 V (with unit).

practice_questions.text: A step-up transformer has a primary coil of 500 turns and a secondary coil of 10,000 turns. The primary voltage is 230 V and the primary current is 20 A. Assuming 100% efficiency, calculate (a) the secondary voltage and (b) the secondary current.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both parts correct with full working shown and units stated. (a) Vs = 230 × (10000/500) = 4600 V. (b) Is = (230 × 20)/4600 = 1.0 A. Secure: Both answers correct but one step missing or unit omitted on one answer. Developing: Correct method for (a) only, or correct substitution into VpIp = VsIs but arithmetic error in (b). Emerging: Turns-ratio equation stated but incorrect rearrangement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the National Grid at very high voltages rather than at the voltages generated at the power station.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: High voltage → low current (1 mark); power lost in cables = I²R (1 mark); smaller current reduces power lost as heat (1 mark); step-up transformer at power station raises voltage for transmission (1 mark). Secure: Three of four points clearly linked. Developing: States high voltage reduces current but does not connect this to I²R or power loss. Emerging: Vague reference to 'less energy is wasted' without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of transformers in the electrical power transmission system, referring to both the advantages of high-voltage transmission and any limitations of real-world transformers.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument covering: high-voltage transmission reduces I²R losses significantly; step-up at power station and step-down near consumers explained; real transformers lose some energy as heat in the core (eddy currents) and in coil resistance, so 100% efficiency is an idealisation; overall judgement that transformers are highly effective — modern designs achieve very high efficiency — making the benefits far outweigh the limitations. Secure: Both advantages and limitations addressed with correct physics but conclusion less well justified. Developing: Advantages well described; limitations superficial. Emerging: Mentions transformers change voltage but limited analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly identifies the products of an acid + metal carbonate reaction?
A) Salt + hydrogen
B) Salt + water
C) Salt + water + carbon dioxide
D) Salt + oxygen + water
practice_questions.marks: C) Salt + water + carbon dioxide [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Name the salt produced when magnesium reacts with sulfuric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Magnesium sulfate [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A student prepares a pure, dry sample of copper(II) sulfate. Describe the method the student should use, including the key steps for obtaining pure, dry crystals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Warm dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker [1]; add excess copper(II) oxide (black powder) to ensure all acid reacts [1]; stir until no more dissolves [1]; filter to remove excess unreacted copper(II) oxide [1]; evaporate the blue filtrate gently until crystals begin to form [1]; leave to crystallise fully and pat dry with filter paper [1].
Secure (3–4): Correct steps but missing the reason for using excess base (it ensures all the acid reacts) or the evaporation detail.
Developing (1–2): Identifies filtering and evaporating but omits the key reason for using excess base.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'concordant results' in a titration and explain why only concordant results are used to calculate the mean titre.
practice_questions.marks: Concordant results are two or more titres that agree within 0.10 cm³ of each other [1]. They are used because they show the experiment is reproducible and precise [1]. Results that are anomalous (the rough titre or any outlier) are excluded to avoid skewing the average and reducing accuracy [1].

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.20 mol/dm³ was neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Moles NaOH = 0.20 × 0.025 = 0.005 mol [1 mark]. Ratio NaOH : HCl = 1 : 1 (from NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O), so moles HCl = 0.005 mol [1 mark]. Concentration HCl = 0.005 ÷ 0.020 = 0.25 mol/dm³ [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between making a soluble salt by neutralisation and making an insoluble salt by precipitation. Include the steps for each method.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Soluble salt — acid reacted with excess insoluble base [1], filtered to remove excess solid [1], filtrate evaporated and crystallised to give the salt [1]. Insoluble salt — two solutions containing the required ions are mixed [1], the insoluble salt precipitates immediately from solution [1], the precipitate is filtered off, washed with distilled water and dried [1].
Secure (3–4): One method correct in full, other partially.
Developing (1–2): Identifies filtering for one method without explaining the logic of excess for soluble route or precipitation for insoluble route.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct definition of a pathogen?
A) A white blood cell that produces antibodies
B) A microorganism that causes disease
C) A molecule on the surface of a host cell
D) An enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls
practice_questions.marks: B) A microorganism that causes disease [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between the lytic and lysogenic replication cycles of a virus.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for:
• Lytic: virus immediately replicates inside the host cell then bursts (lyses) it to release new virus particles.
• Lysogenic: viral DNA integrates into the host cell genome and is replicated passively with the cell; can remain dormant before switching to lytic.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how vaccination prevents a person from developing symptoms of a disease when they encounter the pathogen for the second time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Vaccine introduces dead/weakened pathogen or antigens; lymphocytes produce complementary antibodies and memory lymphocytes form; on second exposure memory lymphocytes enable rapid division and a large antibody response; antibodies bind antigens before infection establishes — student links each step causally.
Secure: At least three steps explained causally.
Developing: Vaccine/antibodies mentioned, memory cells described, but causal chain incomplete.
Emerging: Simple factual points; no causal chain.
[4 marks — one mark per linked explanatory step]

practice_questions.text:
A student is investigating the effectiveness of three different antibiotics against a bacterial strain. They place antibiotic-soaked paper discs on an agar plate seeded with the bacteria and incubate for 48 hours.

Explain what the student should measure and how the results would indicate which antibiotic is most effective.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for:
• Measure the diameter (or area) of the zone of inhibition — the clear area around each disc where bacteria have not grown.
• A larger zone of inhibition indicates the antibiotic is more effective at killing or inhibiting that bacterial strain.
• Results should be repeated to check reproducibility and reduce the effect of anomalies.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Herd immunity is described as protecting individuals who cannot be vaccinated. Explain why a high vaccination rate in a population is necessary to protect these vulnerable individuals.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A high proportion of immune individuals means an infected person is likely to encounter only immune people; the pathogen cannot establish chains of transmission; spread through the population is broken before it reaches unvaccinated individuals; specific threshold (herd immunity threshold) must be met.
Secure: Chain of transmission broken because most contacts are immune; unvaccinated individuals therefore rarely exposed.
Developing: Fewer people to spread to, but mechanism not clearly stated.
Emerging: Vague reference to fewer infections.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Cholera is a bacterial disease spread through contaminated water. Malaria is caused by a protist spread by mosquito vectors.

Compare the methods used to control the spread of these two diseases.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cholera controlled by treating water supplies (chlorination, filtration), improving sanitation to prevent faecal contamination, oral rehydration therapy for treatment, hand hygiene — all targeting the water transmission route. Malaria controlled by targeting the mosquito vector: insecticide-treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, draining standing water to eliminate breeding sites, antimalarial prophylaxis and treatment — none of these would work for cholera. Student makes explicit cross-comparison of why the methods differ.
Secure: At least two cholera control methods and two malaria control methods explained with reference to their respective transmission routes.
Developing: Methods listed for both diseases with partial reference to transmission.
Emerging: One or two methods mentioned for each, mostly descriptive.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text:
What is the size range of nanoparticles?
A) 1–10 nm
B) 1–100 nm
C) 100–1000 nm
D) 1–100 µm
Explain why nanoparticles are more chemically reactive than the same substance in bulk form.
practice_questions.marks: Nanoparticles have a much higher surface area to volume ratio [1]; so a greater proportion of atoms are on the surface and available to react [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe one use of nanoparticles in medicine and explain why nanoparticles are suitable for this application.
practice_questions.marks:
Use: drug delivery to cancer cells / wound dressings with silver nanoparticles / antimicrobial clothing [1]. Explanation: their tiny size allows them to enter cells or cross biological barriers [1]; high surface area makes them more effective than bulk materials of the same substance [1].
(Accept any one well-described use with two linked explanatory points.)

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of soda glass and borosilicate glass, and explain why borosilicate glass is preferred for laboratory equipment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear comparison of both glasses on at least two properties, with a causal explanation linked to use.
Secure: Two properties compared, one explanation.
Developing: One property compared or one use stated.
Emerging: Simple relevant point.

Credit points:
• Soda glass: lower melting point, cheaper [1]
• Borosilicate: higher melting point / greater thermal shock resistance [1]
• Borosilicate preferred because lab glassware is heated and cooled rapidly [1]
• Soda glass would crack under rapid temperature change [1]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is choosing between GFRP (fibreglass) and CFRP (carbon fibre) for making the body of a high-performance racing car.
(a) State one property that both GFRP and CFRP share. [1]
(b) Explain why CFRP might be preferred despite being more expensive. [2]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Both are strong / lightweight / have high strength-to-weight ratio / are corrosion-resistant [1 for any one].
(b) CFRP is stiffer and stronger than GFRP [1]; lower mass improves vehicle performance / speed / fuel efficiency, justifying the higher cost [1].

practice_questions.text: The use of nanoparticles in consumer products has increased significantly. Some scientists argue that products containing nanoparticles should be restricted until more safety research has been done. Evaluate this view, considering both the benefits of nanoparticles and the health concerns associated with their use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with specific examples of benefits and risks; justified conclusion referencing precautionary principle or ongoing research.
Secure: Two or more benefits and at least one risk with explanation; some evaluation.
Developing: Benefits or risks described but not both; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Simple points without explanation.

Credit points (any 6):
• Nanoparticles have genuine benefits: effective UV protection in sunscreen, drug targeting in medicine, antimicrobial wound dressings [1 per distinct example, max 2]
• Their high surface area to volume ratio is the source of enhanced properties [1]
• Small size allows nanoparticles to enter cells and cross biological barriers, potentially causing harm [1]
• Long-term health effects are not yet fully understood [1]
• Precautionary principle: act cautiously when risks uncertain [1]
• Restricting use could slow beneficial medical applications [1]
• Continued research would allow better risk assessment before wider use [1]
• Justified conclusion weighing benefits against risks [1]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes an alpha particle?
A) A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
B) An electromagnetic wave emitted from the nucleus
C) Two protons and two neutrons bound together
D) A neutron emitted from the nucleus
practice_questions.marks: C) Two protons and two neutrons bound together [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the atomic (proton) number and mass (nucleon) number changes that occur during beta-minus decay.
practice_questions.marks: Proton number increases by 1 [1 mark]; mass (nucleon) number stays the same / unchanged [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 6,400 Bq. The half-life of the isotope is 8 hours. Calculate the activity after 24 hours.
practice_questions.marks: 24 hours ÷ 8 hours = 3 half-lives [1 mark]. 6400 → 3200 → 1600 → 800 Bq [1 mark for correct sequence or calculation]. Activity = 800 Bq [1 mark + unit].

practice_questions.text:
Complete and balance the following nuclear equation for the alpha decay of polonium-210:
²¹⁰₈₄Po → ___X + ⁴₂He
Identify the element X, giving its mass number and proton number.
practice_questions.marks: Mass number of X: 210 − 4 = 206 [1 mark]. Proton number of X: 84 − 2 = 82 [1 mark]. Element X is lead (Pb) [1 mark]. Written as ²⁰⁶₈₂Pb [1 mark for fully correct notation].

practice_questions.text: Explain how the results of the gold foil experiment led scientists to change the model of the atom from the plum pudding model to the nuclear model.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): explains what was expected (most alpha particles to be slightly deflected by a uniform positive charge) and what was actually observed (most went straight through; some deflected at large angles; a very few bounced back), then links each observation to a specific conclusion (empty space; small dense nucleus; nucleus is positively charged and repels alpha particles). Secure (3–4): explains the key observations and at least two structural conclusions. Developing (2): mentions large-angle deflection and nucleus. Emerging (1): states that the plum pudding model was disproved.

practice_questions.text: A hospital uses a radioactive isotope to treat a patient. The activity of the sample must be between 50 Bq and 100 Bq when it is used. The sample has an initial activity of 6,400 Bq and a half-life of 6 hours. Calculate the number of hours from preparation that the sample is suitable for use. Show all your working.
