practice_questions.marks: Half-life sequence: 6400 → 3200 (6 h) → 1600 (12 h) → 800 (18 h) → 400 (24 h) → 200 (30 h) → 100 (36 h) → 50 (42 h) [1 mark per correct step, up to 3 marks]. Suitable range: activity is 100 Bq at 36 h and 50 Bq at 42 h [1 mark]. Therefore suitable for use between 36 and 42 hours after preparation [1 mark]. Allow ECF from the half-life sequence. [1 mark for unit consistency].

practice_questions.text: State Fick's law of diffusion and identify one feature of the alveolus that maximises the rate of diffusion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area × concentration difference ÷ membrane thickness. 1 mark: Any one correctly identified and explained feature — e.g. large surface area (millions of alveoli); thin walls (one cell thick, short diffusion distance); dense capillary network (maintains steep concentration gradient).

practice_questions.text: A patient has a resting heart rate of 60 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 80 cm³. Calculate their cardiac output in cm³ per minute. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Correct substitution into cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (80 × 60). 1 mark: Final answer 4800 cm³ per minute with correct unit.

practice_questions.text: Compare the structure of an artery with that of a vein. Explain how each structure is adapted to the vessel's function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arteries — thick muscular/elastic walls withstand high blood pressure from heartbeat; no valves needed as pressure maintains flow direction; veins — thinner walls as blood pressure is low; valves prevent backflow of blood moving slowly back to the heart; all four structural-function links present.
Secure: Three correct structure-function links across both vessels.
Developing: Two correct points, one from each vessel, with basic explanation.
Emerging: One correct point with limited structure-function linkage.

practice_questions.text: During a 10-kilometre run, a runner's muscles begin to fatigue and feel painful towards the end of the race. Explain why this happens, using your knowledge of respiration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Muscles require more energy; oxygen delivery cannot keep pace with demand; cells switch to anaerobic respiration; glucose is only partially broken down; lactate accumulates in muscle cells; lactate causes muscle fatigue and the sensation of burning pain.
Secure: Four of the six points above with correct causal linkage.
Developing: Identifies anaerobic respiration and lactate accumulation without full causal chain.
Emerging: States muscles run out of oxygen with limited explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how red blood cells are adapted for their function of transporting oxygen.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Biconcave disc shape increases surface area for oxygen uptake (increases rate of diffusion). 1 mark: Contain haemoglobin, which binds reversibly to oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin. 1 mark: No nucleus, leaving more space for haemoglobin molecules, maximising oxygen-carrying capacity.

practice_questions.text: A scientist measures the rate of gas exchange across a membrane in two conditions: one with a thin membrane (0.5 µm) and one with a thick membrane (2 µm). The surface area and concentration difference are kept the same. Use Fick's law to calculate and compare the relative rates of diffusion in each condition.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly states Fick's law; identifies that rate ∝ 1 ÷ membrane thickness (surface area and concentration difference held constant); calculates that the thin membrane gives 4× the rate of the thick membrane (2 ÷ 0.5 = 4); correctly interprets this as the thin membrane allowing faster exchange; relates this to alveolar or capillary adaptations in a living system; answer clearly annotated with units and reasoning.
Secure: Correct calculation with ratio stated and biological link made.
Developing: Correct ratio calculated but biological application absent or vague.
Emerging: Identifies that thinner membrane gives faster diffusion without calculation.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a community and a population.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: A population is all the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time. 1 mark: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting together in the same habitat.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use a quadrat and random sampling to estimate the percentage cover of daisies in a field of 100 m². Include how you would ensure your results were representative.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses random number table or app to generate coordinates; places quadrat at each coordinate; counts number of squares/percentage of quadrat covered by daisies; repeats for a minimum of 10 quadrats (more for reliability); calculates mean percentage cover; control variables include quadrat size, time of sampling; acknowledges any source of sampling bias.
Secure: Method involves random coordinates, multiple quadrats, a measurement of coverage and calculation of a mean.
Developing: Uses quadrats but method for randomisation or mean calculation is incomplete.
Emerging: States use a quadrat with limited method.

practice_questions.text: Explain how eutrophication following fertiliser run-off can reduce the biodiversity of a river ecosystem. Use a chain of events in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fertiliser (nitrates/phosphates) enters river; algae grow rapidly forming an algal bloom; algae block sunlight reaching underwater plants, which die; decomposers break down dead plants, consuming dissolved oxygen; oxygen levels fall; fish and other aquatic organisms die; biodiversity falls.
Secure: Four of the six steps in the chain, correctly ordered.
Developing: Two or three steps with correct logic but missing key links.
Emerging: States that fertiliser harms the river with one correct point.

practice_questions.text: A food chain in a woodland is: Oak tree → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk. If the oak trees contain 80,000 kJ of energy, and the transfer efficiency between each trophic level is 10%, calculate how much energy is available to the sparrowhawk.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Energy at caterpillar level = 80,000 × 10/100 = 8,000 kJ. 1 mark: Energy at blue tit level = 8,000 × 10/100 = 800 kJ. 1 mark: Energy at sparrowhawk level = 800 × 10/100 = 80 kJ. Award ECF if one early error is carried through correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the carbon in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can end up as carbon in the body of a decomposer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A plant removes CO₂ from the atmosphere during photosynthesis and converts it into organic molecules (e.g. glucose, then proteins/fats in the plant body); an animal eats the plant and takes carbon into its own body through digestion and assimilation; the animal dies; a decomposer (bacterium or fungus) feeds on the dead animal by secreting digestive enzymes; carbon is incorporated into the decomposer's body.
Secure: Three of the four steps with correct causal links.
Developing: Two steps, one involving photosynthesis and one involving a consumer or decomposer.
Emerging: States that plants take in CO₂ with little further detail.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of maintaining high biodiversity for the long-term sustainability of ecosystems and human food security.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines biodiversity; explains that high biodiversity increases ecosystem stability (more species to fill roles if one declines); discusses threats (deforestation, pollution, climate change, overexploitation); discusses conservation strategies and their effectiveness (breeding programmes, seed banks, habitat restoration, reforestation); links biodiversity to food security through pollinators, natural pest control, genetic diversity of crops; considers trade-offs (conservation vs. land use for farming); reaches a justified conclusion about the relative importance of biodiversity protection.
Secure: Covers definition, threats, at least two conservation strategies and a clear link to food security, with a conclusion.
Developing: Identifies threats and some conservation strategies but does not integrate food security or lacks conclusion.
Emerging: Gives a general account of biodiversity loss without analysis.

before.exam_tip_html: For fieldwork questions, examiners want to see: independent variable (what changes along the transect), dependent variable (what is counted), control variables (same-sized quadrat, same observer criteria), how the data are analysed (calculate mean percentage cover, use statistical tests). For 6-mark ‘Describe a Method’ questions on quadrats, mention random number coordinates to eliminate sampling bias. On eutrophication, trace the full chain of events from fertiliser run-off to fish death — partial chains score partial credit.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the BMI of a person with a mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.80 m. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practice_questions.marks:
BMI = 72 ÷ (1.80)² = 72 ÷ 3.24 = 22 (kg/m²) [2 significant figures]
• 1 mark for correct substitution: 72 ÷ (1.80)² or equivalent
• 1 mark for correct answer: 22 (kg/m²) with units
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what a double-blind placebo trial is and why this design is used when testing new drugs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Neither patient nor clinician knows who receives the drug or placebo; eliminates both placebo effect (patients' belief in treatment affecting outcomes) and observer bias (clinician's expectations affecting assessment); comparison group (placebo) allows true effect of drug to be measured statistically; result is more reliable.
Secure: Double-blind defined correctly; at least two reasons for the design.
Developing: Double-blind partially defined; one reason given.
Emerging: Placebo mentioned but no explanation of why bias matters.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced in the laboratory.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for:
• A mouse is immunised with the target antigen so its lymphocytes produce specific antibodies.
• Lymphocytes are fused with myeloma (tumour) cells to produce hybridoma cells.
• Hybridoma cells are cultured; they divide without limit and secrete large quantities of the specific antibody, which is then purified.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A patient with blocked coronary arteries is offered a choice between statin medication and a stent procedure.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each treatment option.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Statins — advantages: non-invasive, daily tablet, lower cholesterol reducing further plaque formation; disadvantages: take time to work, potential muscle side effects, do not clear existing blockage. Stents — advantages: immediate restoration of blood flow, effective for severe narrowing; disadvantages: surgical risk, anaesthetic, does not prevent further build-up elsewhere, anti-clotting medication needed post-op. Sustained evaluative comparison: student weighs which is preferable given severity of blockage and patient factors; reaches justified conclusion that severe blockage requires stent + long-term statins and lifestyle change.
Secure: Clear benefits and limitations of both; some comparative weighing; conclusion present.
Developing: Benefits and limitations for each listed; little weighing or comparison; conclusion weak.
Emerging: One or two factual points per treatment; no evaluation.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text: A pharmaceutical company discovers a new compound that kills the bacteria that cause tuberculosis. Outline the process the company must follow before the drug can be prescribed to patients.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Preclinical testing on cell cultures and tissues (toxicity, efficacy); if safe, animal testing for dose and side effects; Phase I clinical trial on healthy volunteers (safety, dose range); Phase II on patients with TB (effectiveness, monitor side effects); Phase III large-scale double-blind placebo-controlled trial; statistical analysis; submission to regulatory body; peer review of published results; approval before prescribing.
Secure: At least four stages with preclinical → clinical trial → approval sequence correct.
Developing: Preclinical and clinical testing mentioned; stages not clearly ordered; regulatory approval not mentioned.
Emerging: Vague reference to testing; no sequence.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) State one advantage and one disadvantage of using monoclonal antibodies in cancer treatment compared with conventional chemotherapy.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for:
• Advantage: monoclonal antibodies target only cancer cells displaying the specific antigen, reducing damage to healthy tissue compared with conventional chemotherapy.
• Disadvantage: any one of — expensive to produce; can cause immune reactions in some patients; difficult to find a truly unique tumour antigen; not all cancers have a suitable targetable antigen.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by specific heat capacity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (or 1 K).

practice_questions.text: A student measures the density of an irregularly shaped stone using a measuring cylinder and a balance. Describe the steps the student should take to find the volume of the stone.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Fill the measuring cylinder with a known volume of water and record it. 1 mark: Submerge the stone fully in the water. 1 mark: Record the new water level; the volume of the stone equals the increase in water level (volume displaced).

practice_questions.text: A 2.0 kg block of iron is heated from 20°C to 70°C using an immersion heater. The specific heat capacity of iron is 450 J/kg°C. Calculate the energy transferred to the iron.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct substitution: Q = 2.0 × 450 × 50. 1 mark for correct answer: Q = 45,000 J (with unit, accept 45 kJ).

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why the temperature of a substance does not change while it is melting, even though energy is continuously being supplied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Energy is used to break the bonds (forces) between particles (1 mark) rather than increase their kinetic energy (1 mark); kinetic energy determines temperature (1 mark); so temperature stays constant until all bonds are broken and the substance is fully melted (1 mark). Secure: Three correct points with particle-level language. Developing: States temperature is constant and energy is used, but does not link to particle bonds or kinetic energy. Emerging: Vague reference to energy being used without particle explanation.

practice_questions.text: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 0.40 m³ at a pressure of 150,000 Pa. The gas is compressed to a volume of 0.10 m³ at the same temperature. Calculate the new pressure of the gas. State the law you are using.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating Boyle's law / p1V1 = p2V2 (with condition: constant temperature, fixed mass). 1 mark for correct substitution: 150000 × 0.40 = p2 × 0.10. 1 mark for correct answer: p2 = 600,000 Pa (or 600 kPa).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the particle model as an explanation for the properties of solids, liquids, and gases. In your answer, consider the strengths and limitations of the model.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument covering strengths (explains density differences in terms of particle spacing; explains changes of state; predicts gas behaviour such as Boyle's law from collision frequency; explains latent heat as bond breaking); limitations (treats particles as identical spheres with no internal structure; does not account for intermolecular forces in detail; cannot explain all properties of real gases at very high pressures or low temperatures); justified conclusion that the model is highly useful at GCSE level but is a simplification. Secure: Strengths and limitations both addressed with specific examples; conclusion present but less well justified. Developing: Strengths described well; limitations superficial. Emerging: Describes particle arrangements in each state only.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly explains why alpha sources are used in household smoke alarms?
A) Alpha particles penetrate through the housing to detect smoke outside
B) Alpha particles ionise the air between electrodes; smoke absorbs them, reducing the current
C) Alpha particles are reflected by smoke particles, triggering the alarm
D) Alpha particles are weakly ionising, making them safe for household use
practice_questions.marks: B) Alpha particles ionise the air between electrodes; smoke absorbs them, reducing the current [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between contamination and irradiation, and state which is generally more dangerous and why.
practice_questions.marks: Irradiation: exposure to radiation from an external source; stops when source removed; person/object does not become radioactive [1 mark]. Contamination: radioactive material on or inside the body; continuous exposure even after leaving the original source [1 mark]. Contamination is generally more dangerous [1 mark] because the source remains close to cells and continues to irradiate them, with no way to remove the exposure [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why the moderator and the control rods in a nuclear reactor serve different functions.
practice_questions.marks: Moderator slows neutrons to speeds at which they are most effective at triggering fission in U-235 [1 mark]; without it, fast neutrons are less likely to cause fission [1 mark]. Control rods absorb neutrons to regulate the rate of the chain reaction [1 mark]; inserting them further reduces the reaction rate and withdrawing them increases it [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A patient is given a radioactive tracer for a PET scan. Explain why the tracer used must have a short half-life, and why it must be produced nearby.
practice_questions.marks: Short half-life: the tracer decays quickly after the scan, reducing the patient’s total radiation dose [1 mark]. Also, rapid decay means high initial activity, providing a detectable signal without requiring a large quantity of radioactive material [1 mark]. Produced nearby: because the half-life is short (e.g. approximately 110 minutes for fluorine-18), the tracer would decay significantly during transport [1 mark]; it must be used within hours of production, so a cyclotron must be located close to the scanning facility [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear fission as an energy source compared to burning fossil fuels.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): balanced evaluation covers: advantages of fission (no CO2 during operation, high energy density, reliable baseload power, finite but long-lasting uranium supply) and disadvantages (radioactive waste, long storage periods, high construction and decommissioning costs, public perception and safety risk, low-probability but high-consequence accidents). Fossil fuel advantages (established infrastructure, dispatchable, relatively cheap) and disadvantages (CO2 contributing to climate change, air pollution, finite supply, price volatility). Justified conclusion that neither is ideal; the best choice depends on balancing climate targets against waste and safety concerns. Secure (3–4): develops both sides with specific points. Developing (2): lists points without evaluative comparison. Emerging (1): simple relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why nuclear fusion requires extremely high temperatures to occur, and describe the main challenge this creates for building a practical fusion reactor.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): explains that at low temperatures protons (nuclei) repel each other due to electrostatic repulsion between positive charges [1]; high temperature gives nuclei sufficient kinetic energy to overcome this repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to take over and cause fusion [1]; at these temperatures matter exists as a plasma that cannot be contained by physical materials [1]; must be confined by magnetic fields (e.g. in a tokamak) or laser compression [1]; achieving net energy gain (output > input) has not yet been demonstrated at power-plant scale [1]; the economic and engineering barriers make commercial fusion still distant [1]. Secure (3–4): explains repulsion and temperature requirement plus one containment point. Developing (2): explains the temperature requirement. Emerging (1): states that high temperature is needed.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly identifies what happens at the cathode during electrolysis?
A) Negative ions are oxidised
B) Positive ions gain electrons and are reduced
C) Positive ions lose electrons and are oxidised
D) Negative ions gain electrons and are reduced
practice_questions.marks: B) Positive ions gain electrons and are reduced [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: State why aluminium oxide is dissolved in cryolite before electrolysis.
practice_questions.marks: To lower the melting point [1 mark], reducing the energy required and making the process less expensive.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Write the half-equation for the reaction occurring at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide.
practice_questions.marks: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb [1 mark for correct product, 1 mark for balanced electrons and charge]. The lead(II) ions are reduced — they gain electrons at the cathode.

practice_questions.text: During the electrolysis of copper sulfate solution using copper electrodes, explain what happens to the mass of each electrode and the concentration of copper(II) ions in solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): The copper cathode gains mass because Cu²⁺ ions from solution are reduced and deposited as copper metal [1 mark]. The copper anode loses mass because copper atoms are oxidised and dissolve as Cu²⁺ ions into the solution [1 mark]. Because Cu²⁺ ions are removed at the cathode and replenished by the anode dissolving at equal rates, the concentration of copper(II) ions in solution remains approximately constant [2 marks].
Secure (2–3): Correctly identifies cathode and anode mass changes but does not explain the effect on ion concentration.
Developing (1): Mentions cathode deposits copper without explaining the anode dissolving.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the carbon anodes in aluminium extraction must be replaced regularly.
practice_questions.marks: Oxygen is produced at the anode [1 mark]. The oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anodes, forming carbon dioxide [1 mark]. This gradually burns the anodes away, reducing their size until they must be replaced [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: In an electrolysis experiment, a student electrolyses a solution of sodium chloride using inert electrodes. Predict and explain the products formed at each electrode.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): At the cathode — Na⁺ ions are present but sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions from water are discharged preferentially [1 mark]. Hydrogen gas is produced [1 mark]. Half-equation: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ [1 mark]. At the anode — Cl⁻ ions are present (a halide), so chlorine gas is produced preferentially rather than oxygen [1 mark]. Half-equation: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ [1 mark]. Observation: chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper; hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop [1 mark].
Secure (3–4): Correctly identifies one electrode product with explanation; other partially explained.
Developing (1–2): States 'hydrogen and chlorine' without explaining the discharge rules.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly defines potable water?
A) Water containing no dissolved substances
B) Water that is safe to drink but may contain low levels of dissolved minerals
C) Water that has been boiled and condensed
D) Water treated only by filtration
State the three stages of treating fresh water in the UK to produce potable water, in the correct order.
practice_questions.marks:
Sedimentation [1]; filtration [1]; chlorination [1].
(Must be in this order for full marks; accept reasonable synonyms but must be three distinct stages.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why desalination is used in some countries but not in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Some countries lack sufficient fresh water sources (rivers, reservoirs) [1]; desalination converts sea water to potable water but requires much more energy than treating fresh water [1].
(Accept: UK has adequate rainfall/fresh water so fresh water treatment is cheaper and lower energy.)

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a life-cycle assessment (LCA) and state one limitation of using LCA data.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation of LCA covering all four stages with a specific limitation linked to data reliability.
Secure: Three stages of LCA explained; limitation stated.
Developing: LCA partially described; limitation vague.
Emerging: One stage or simple statement.

Credit points:
• LCA assesses environmental impact at every stage of a product's life [1]
• Stages include: raw material extraction; manufacture; use; disposal [1 per stage, max 2 — must name at least two]
• Limitation: LCAs can be subjective / data may be selectively chosen / different weightings give different results [1]

practice_questions.text: A local council is deciding whether to supply water using a new desalination plant or by expanding its existing reservoir and water treatment works. Evaluate the two options, considering environmental impact, cost, and reliability of water supply.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation of both options across all three criteria with a justified recommendation.
Secure: Both options addressed on at least two criteria; some evaluation.
Developing: One option described in detail; comparison limited.
Emerging: Simple relevant points without comparison.

Credit points (any 6):
• Reservoir treatment: lower energy cost / lower environmental impact from energy use [1]
• Reservoir treatment: depends on sufficient rainfall — less reliable in drought conditions [1]
• Desalination: higher energy cost [1]
• Desalination: produces potable water from sea water — reliable regardless of rainfall [1]
• Desalination: greater CO₂ emissions unless powered by renewables [1]
• Expanding reservoir: may disturb land/habitat [1]
• Justified recommendation with reasoning (e.g. expand reservoir where rainfall adequate; desalination for arid regions) [1]

practice_questions.text: Recycling aluminium uses considerably less energy than producing it from its ore. Using this example, explain the benefits of recycling finite resources. In your answer, consider both the environmental and economic arguments.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Environmental and economic benefits clearly linked to the aluminium example; balanced, with acknowledgement of recycling's own costs.
Secure: Two or more benefits with explanation; limited acknowledgement of drawbacks.
Developing: Benefits listed without clear explanation or linkage to aluminium.
Emerging: Simple points.

Credit points (any 6):
• Aluminium ore is a finite resource — will eventually run out [1]
• Recycling reduces need to mine (extract) more ore [1]
• Significant energy saving compared to electrolysis of aluminium oxide [1]
• Lower energy use means lower costs for manufacturers [1]
• Reduced CO₂ emissions from energy production [1]
• Less waste to landfill [1]
• Recycling does have costs: collection, sorting, transport [1]
• Overall, recycling aluminium conserves resources and is economically viable [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an exothermic and an endothermic reaction in terms of energy transfer to or from the surroundings.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clearly distinguishes both types by direction of energy transfer; links to bond breaking (endothermic) and bond making (exothermic); explains why temperature of surroundings rises or falls; includes precise scientific vocabulary throughout.
Secure: States direction of energy transfer for both types; explains temperature change; may not fully develop bond-energy reasoning.
Developing: Identifies one type correctly with temperature change; explanation of the other is partial or missing.
Emerging: Names one type with limited or no explanation of energy transfer.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) The table below gives bond energies for the reaction: \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3\). Bond energies: N≡N = 945 kJ/mol; H–H = 436 kJ/mol; N–H = 391 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change for this reaction. Show your working clearly and give the sign and units in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct energy to break bonds (945 + 3 × 436 = 2253 kJ/mol). 1 mark: correct energy released making bonds (6 × 391 = 2346 kJ/mol). 1 mark: correct overall change with sign and units (ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol, exothermic). ECF applies if arithmetic error in step 1 or 2.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is shown by an exothermic reaction profile, including how the activation energy and overall energy change are represented on the diagram.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: reactants at higher energy level than products. 1 mark: activation energy is the height from reactant energy level to the peak. 1 mark: overall energy change is the difference in height between reactants and products, with energy released shown as a downward arrow or negative value.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by activation energy.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the minimum energy that reacting particles must have (possess / collide with) for a reaction to occur (for a collision to be successful).

practice_questions.text: A student uses bond energies to calculate the energy change for a reaction and gets +250 kJ/mol. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Explain what this value tells you about the bond energies involved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: endothermic. 1 mark: the energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants is greater than the energy released when bonds form in the products (by 250 kJ/mol).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction. In your answer, refer to activation energy and reaction profiles.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway; lower activation energy means a greater proportion of collisions have sufficient energy; links to rate profile showing lower peak; notes overall energy change is unchanged.
Secure: States catalyst lowers activation energy; links to more successful collisions; may not mention unchanged overall energy change.
Developing: States catalyst lowers activation energy without linking to collision frequency or the profile.
Emerging: States catalyst speeds up reaction without reference to activation energy or energy profiles.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a piece of evidence that supports the heliocentric model of the Solar System over the geocentric model?
A) The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west every day
B) Galileo observed four moons orbiting Jupiter in 1610
C) Stars appear to move across the sky during the year
D) The Moon has phases as seen from Earth
practice_questions.marks: B) Galileo observed four moons orbiting Jupiter in 1610 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the correct order of stages in the life cycle of a star of similar mass to the Sun.
practice_questions.marks: Nebula [1 mark] → (protostar →) main sequence star → red giant [1 mark] → (planetary nebula →) white dwarf [1 mark]. Accept any order that correctly places nebula first, main sequence second, red giant third and white dwarf last. Protostar/planetary nebula as intermediate stages also acceptable.

practice_questions.text: Explain what red shift is and what the observation that all distant galaxies show red shift tells us about the Universe.
practice_questions.marks: Red shift: light from galaxies moving away has a longer wavelength / shifted towards the red end of the spectrum compared to laboratory sources [1 mark]. The shift is caused by the Doppler effect — galaxies moving away stretch the wavelength of their emitted light [1 mark]. All distant galaxies show red shift, meaning all are moving away from us [1 mark]. The greater the distance, the larger the red shift, showing the Universe is expanding [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Compare the Big Bang theory and the Steady State theory. Explain which piece of evidence led to the Big Bang theory being the currently accepted model.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): explains Big Bang (universe originated in a hot dense point, has expanded ever since) and Steady State (universe has always existed, new matter created as galaxies separate); both account for red shift [1 each]; CMB is uniform microwave radiation detected in all directions, consistent with leftover heat from an initial hot dense state [1]; Steady State cannot explain why CMB exists [1]; more evidence supports Big Bang so it is the accepted model [1]. Secure (3–4): explains both theories with the CMB as decisive evidence. Developing (2): defines one theory and mentions CMB. Emerging (1): states the Big Bang theory is accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the balance between gravity and radiation pressure determines the stability of a main sequence star, and explain what happens to this balance when the star runs out of hydrogen fuel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): gravity pulls material inward towards the core; nuclear fusion in the core generates outward radiation pressure; on the main sequence these two forces are in balance, so the star is stable [2]; when hydrogen fuel runs low, fusion rate decreases and outward pressure drops; gravity causes the core to contract and heat further; the outer layers expand and cool to form a red giant (for a solar-mass star) [2]; this process continues until the star can no longer sustain fusion and the outer layers are shed [1]; if the star is massive enough, the core collapses catastrophically in a supernova [1]. Secure (3–4): explains balance and what happens when hydrogen runs out. Developing (2): mentions gravity and fusion pressure in balance. Emerging (1): states fusion is the energy source.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which methods of observing the Universe have changed over time and explain one advantage of placing telescopes above the Earth's atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks: Way 1: from naked eye observation to optical telescopes (from seventeenth century), allowing much more detailed observation of fainter objects and planetary features [1 mark]. Way 2: development of radio, X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes allowing observation across the whole electromagnetic spectrum, not just visible light [1 mark]. Advantage: above the atmosphere, there is no atmospheric absorption of certain wavelengths (e.g. X-rays are absorbed by the atmosphere); telescopes outside the atmosphere can detect radiation that never reaches the ground [1 mark]. Also: no atmospheric distortion (twinkling) so images are sharper [1 mark — accept any one well-explained advantage].
